SISTER SERAPH INE,
JULIAN CORBETT. (Author of "A Basineskin Great Waters," cbc.)
PART lIL XIV.

So it came as Sister Seraphine knew from the firstAt would, and she waited for it on her knees. On her knees upon the faldstool before the Madonna, praying her little prayers continually, and trying to make them mean something. But there was nothing but words. Her thoughts, dis- tracted by the long vigil, would not turn heaven- ward. It was along the causeway they were strained listening—listening for the sound of wheels and hoofs. And it came at last, faint and musical at first, but still she cmld not pray, for every moment it grew louder and nearer, tillsheeould hear distinct from the rattle of the wheels the eight hoofs beat- ing confusedly upon the stones. "Holy Mother," she began ao-ain, but now the horses trod together and then they lost step again, and 'always the clatter grew nearer and louder and chased away her prayers, till the sharp ring of iron striking and scraping upon the causeway told her the Baron had reined in smartly at the gate. "Holy Mother !" she began again. "Take them into the shade, Robert," said his hard voice. "I shall not be out for an hour." "Holy Mother, who thyself—" ' "And if the flies fret the mare, walk them a bit. I don't want herto start kicking again." "Holy Mother, who thyself didst know sorrow—" but the rest was his firm tread upon the path be. tween the roses, and she could only count his paces he drew near the door. "Sister Seraphine awaits you in her room," she heard the voice of Sister Theodora say, and her heart sank. Yes, she who hul renounced the world was waiting there alone, and he who had drank liie to the dregs—he was•coming, step by step, up the stairs to feast his eyes upon her beauty. She was woman enough to know that, and it was the crown of her misery; and when suddenly she saw him in the doorway with his bristling mous- tache and faultless frock coat, do what she would, she could not hold back a burning blush that arrayed her beauty in ite most enchanting dress.

div.head: XV.
div.p: XV.

The Baron had expected a great deal, but his first glance showed him something more than he expected. He admitted to himself without any -hesitation, that in all his wide experience he had never seen anything quite so fine, and he bowed low in homage. "Madam," said he, in his most engaging tone, "permit me to thank you a thousand times for the privilege of this interview." "I desire no thanks, sir," she said, trembling, and never raising her eyes as she returned his bow. "It is entirely a matter of business. Pray be seated." "Nay, Madam," said he, "we must not sit in the presence of angels." Then she looked up at him quickly, but when she saw how he gazed at her with hi a dissipated air, she dropped her eyes again, flushing more painfully than before. It was but a moment's glance, half imploring, half terror-stricken; but for him it was enough to revual the full measure of her beauty. He had certainly never seen such eyes. "Pray. sir," she said, as soon as her beating heart would allow, "remember you speak with one who has give!) herself to God." "1 conld rather believe. Madam," the Baron replied, "that God had given himself to you. Where should a man worship, if not here." Once more she looked up to see what he meant. It was onlY too evident, and she dropped her eyes again. "it is clear, sir," said she, trying bravely to steady her voice, "that I must not look to you for the respect which others give to women who like ourselves, have renounced the world. For myself God knows it is little respect I deserve—yet your insults are none the less hard to bear." Madam," broke in the Baron, a little startled.' " I assure you, you misinterpret the feelings with which—" "I think not, sir, indeed ; " she said, as he hesi- tated, speaking still in a low voice and never looking up. "But it matters little. Say what you wish since it is God's will that this should be my punishment. But for pity's sake be merci- ful."

" Really, Madam—" began the Baron quite amazed at his reception and ready to laugh aloud to find himself posed as Heaven's chastening instrument; but one more look at Sister Seraphine, as she stood trembling beside the faldstool with down-east eyes, made the humorous side of the situation less obvious, and with increased astonish- ment he became aware of an awkward silence. It was ridiculous enough—he admitted that to himself—for him of all men to be embarrassed by a shy little nun. As a man of the world he could not allow it. As a man of the world he knew that with women everything was a mere question of impudence—some required more, some less—this little rogue of a nun had clearly not had enough. As aduty to himself she must be mad to talk. "Really, Madam," he began again, "you place me in a very difficult position. What can I say? We have business together. I hear you are beau- tiful, and I come to do my business in person. I find you not only beautiful, but far lovelier than report had lead me to expect. lam surprised into a compliment and you call it an insult! Did you remember the power you have, you would not be so harsh. Do you think such beauty as yours can be concealed! You think, perhaps, it is hidden under the monstrous disguise you are compelled to wear. But for me, madam, it is no veil. I have eaten of the tree of knowledge and my eyes reveal for me true beauty, however cunningly it be covered, and I confess, madam, I have been moved more than I care to own to any but yourself." "Proceed sir," said Sister Seraphine in a low voice as he paused; "I must bear all that Heaven sends." "Madam, madam," burst out the Baron with some warmth, "What folly is this You send to ask me a favour and you deny me everything. I ask as my reward a few minutes' talk with the most beautiful woman I have ever seen, I seek but one kind look from the sweetest eyes in the world—they are yours, and you ref usethem—simply because these rascally priests have tilled your pretty head with their nonsense. Come, be a woman for once. Calm yourself—you are agitated. Let me help you to a seat." He made a movement as though to take her hand, and she, shrinking from it in horror, sank upon her knees before her Madonna. "Holy Mother," she prayed aloud, "plead for me. Great has been my sin and I deserve great punishment. Yet plead for me, Mother, for I can bear no more. Plead that my penance may be anything but this—if not for my sake then for his. Spare him this wickedness that he be stained no deeper with my punishment. For surely he knows not what he does; but Thou, Mother, knowest what I suffer, Thou knowest I can bear no more." She was adorable as she knelt, with clasped hands. and upturned face, pouring out her soul in supplication for him to the simpering Virgin. The whole thing was so naive, too, and the delicacy of her profile was quite extraordinary. She was certainly adorable—and yet he was not enjoying her society. He even began to admit that his joke was falling flat, and to wonder if the flies were fretting the mare, .and if he had not better go. But her face was still upturned, and her lips still moved, and he did not see how to interrupt. It was becoming. less amusing .every minute. Sud- denly be surprised himself by coughing nervously. She rose at once from her knees and looked him calmly in the face,anbmissive still, but without fear. "You had something more to say to me?" she said. "Indeed Madam," replied the Baron, "I have, but I cannot tell how to say it." "You had business with me, had you not? she said, taking the lead quite naturally. "You came to speak of selling us the Hospital." "Say rather, that was my excuse," smiled the Baron with a desperate effort to recover the tone of the interview. "My object was to enjoy a pleasure that you persist in denying me." "Have you no pity ?" she said, quietly. "Madam, I protest," exclaimed the Baron vehemently, "it is you who have no pity! How can I see you standing there and not feel what I do?" "For the love of Heaven, sir," she answered in such deep entreaty as no other man .could have withstood, "have mercy. You do not know what it is you do or you could not persist. But remem- ber what lam, and what you have been. God help you. Ido not reproach you. It is not for that speak of it. For I know it was for what your life has been that God chose you for my punishment. J3ut think what it was for me wito,tllought I had

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: escaped the world when I became- cloistered hers— think what it was to be condemned for my sins to be alone with you. I do not complain, my pride deserves it all, and yet that made it no less hard to bear. What the thought of it has cost me you could never understand, and now my hour has come, and you for a pastime, make my punishment doubly as hard as I dreaded—you make it harder than I have strength to bear. But how could you tell? how could you tell ? " As she finished she covered her beauty with her hands and then there came a little sob. It cannot have been the first time by many that the Baron had made a pretty woman cry, yet the sound disturbed him curiously, and he was clearly con- scious of nothing but an insane desire to have her look at him again, and hear her voice, and watch the beauty of her entreaty. He felt he would give anything to see her again as she was just now and he could think of but one way of getting what he wanted. It was to assume the penitent, and he found he could play the part with a facility so con- vincing al to surprise and even annoy himself.' "Madam," said he, "permit me to ask your pardon, and thank you for your rebuke. As you so generously say, how could I know what I did! I have never seen a woman like you. If I had I might have been another man. Now, I know how badly I have acted in seeking this meeting. I can hardly expect a favour from you, yet, knowing as Ido how good your heart is, I cannot help asking one. I have been guilty, unconsciously indeed, but still guilty of a great injury. Suffer me to atone for it by asking your acceptance of this Hospital. It is a little thing for me to give; but, at least, I can beg of you to accept it in token of my grati- tude to one who has let a rake for once see what goodness may yet be found in a woman." He got what he wanted then • for she left off crying and sat up in her chair, looking gratitude and forgiveness to him out of her brimming eyes. "I knew I was right," she said, with a fine smile of triumph. "I told them that there must yet be in your heart one pure spot. I was sure the Holy Mother would find it." The Baron was enchanted with his success. She was prettier and more confiding than ever. "Then you will accept my gift?" he said, to make her go on talking. "Yes," she answered, with another radiant smile. " Yes ; you have done a noble thing, and I should be happy that God has granted it to me to have helped you tiS it. Truly when His will is most difficult to understand then He is wisest. Who can tell that henceforth you will not be a better man, and be reconciled to the Church? I shall pray for you every day." ' "Will you not pray now?" he asked, losing his head more and more, and knowing only a desire to see her on her knees again, and hear her beseech- ing Heaven for him. "Yes, gladly, if you wish it," she said, happily. She rose at once and went to her faldstool, while he stood close beside her, devouring the beauty of her up-turned face, and drinking the music of her words, till he began to be conscious of %tumultuous feeling, to which he had been long a stranger. To be listening to the childish phrases she was inno- cently pouring forth for his sake as though he were the dearest thing to her on earth; to watch her up-turned face growing each moment more divine; was beyond his self-control. The tumult grew within him, the world around began to lose its reality. There was nothing, but the intent face on which he fed his eyes. Everything else had faded away and did not matter—everything but her faee, a gleam of bewildering beauty in a world of chaos, and for him all existence was centred in one desire. He must kiss the lips that prayed for him. He, too, must taste of heaven ; and, reckless with passion, he bent down to complete his sacrilege. • Steady mare, steady 2" With a loud clatter of hoofs striking on the causeway, the world flashed back again. " Woa then, lass In a moment Sister Seraphine, all unconscious of what she had escaped, was alone at the window, and the baron was flying across the garden without his hat. The gadflies had been too much for the mare, and she had started kicking again.

div.head: XVI.
div.p: XVI.

Thanks to the Baron's promptness he got her head well up before any damage was done, and quickly soothed her ; for he had a wonderful way with animals, and they all took to him, "Just like the women," M. de la Coui,le used to say. Having quieted his trembling mare, the Baron returned. At the gate was a little knot of specta- tors—the Sergeant and Madame Poiton, with Father Andrew, gravely polite and holding a hat in his hand.
"No harm done, Baron, I hope ? " said the Jesuit, pleasantly. " None worth speaking of," answered the Baron.

"lam very glad," said Father Andrew. "It would have seemed hard after your princely generosity; we have heard all about it already from Sister Seraphine. It is really quite princely." "You are too good," said the Baron, making a motion to pass in. "I have brought your hat," said the Jesuit. "Thank you ; but I was going to return." " Indeed ? " "Yes, we had not finished the details when we were interrupted." "That is most unfortunate." "Why unfortunate, Father ? " "Well, because you see it is impossible for you ti return."

"Nonsense, Father ! What do you mean?" "I mean," said the Jesuit, with something of a twinkle in his eye, "that a second interview could not be permitted. You know the dispensation only extended to one."
"But I must make my adieux to the Superior, after quitting her so unceremoniously. It is absurd."
"It is amusing certainly, but the words of the instrument are quite clear. It _Bays an inter- view."
_ "But, Father, you are reslly not serious ? " - •

"Well, hardly 'serious, Barn. The thing is toe ridiculous for that; but I really mean that what you ask is impossible. I will make your excuseF. myself." "It is insufferable," said the Baron, thoroughly out of temper. For a moment he contemplated a rush, hut the stern figure of Sergeant Poiton blocked the way. Turning on his heel, he sum- moned his groom, and, jumping on the box, he lashed the mare savagely across the loins, and was gone without another word.

div.head: XVII.
div.p: XVII.

For some days after this the Baron's temper was unbearable. His servants hardly dared to approach him, until one day his legal adviser came dowm with a nunber of papers, and it was whispered that the Choulines Hospital was no longer the Baron', property. Then he got a little better, but he was still far from himself. No one came to stay at the chateau —not even the yellow-haired lady. Riding and driving were his only recreations, till horses and grooms alike grew weary to death of the Ghoulines Road. What the Baron could see in it, no one could make out, for. everyone knew it was the ugliest road for miles round. They even began to doubt his sanity, when sud- denly he announced his intention of going up to his townhouse.

It was a few nights after this, that as the baron was leaving at an early hour the smoking-room of the Jockey Club, M. de la Course remarked to Count de Selle that he could not make out what had come over Blamberg. "Nor I," said the Count. "He is not half the fellow he used to be."
and what on earth can he want to go to Alaska for, with coverts like his ? " _ _
"lie says," said the Count, "he goes by the doctor's orders."
"I suppose the coverts will not be shoCthis year,. then ?"

"The keepers are to kill the game for the Ghoulines Hospital." "What an extraordinary thing ! Something aunt certainly be wrong with him." "I fancy it is his liver," said the Count. "Well," said M. de la Course, "we will hope his voyage will set him up."
TIIE END.

div.head: Conference at Warrington.
div.p: Conference at Warrington.

The second annual meeting of the Lancashire and Adjacent Counties Conference in connection with tile Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds kAshton Unity) was held at the Conservative Club, Warrington, on Saturday afternoon. Brother J K Gartside, of Charley, (president), occupied the chair and repre- sentatives were present from the Warrington, Charley, Bolton, Hyde, Manchester, Sandbach, Stalybridge, Bebbington, St Helens, Golborne, and Aspull districts. In the course of his address the Chairman said he was sorry they were not able to show the same practical re- sults that they had hoped to be able to show as the effect of the work of the conference. They were in hopes that along with the brethren of the Yorkshire Union they would have been able to have done some- thing for the good of the Order. He thought they bad certainly made their presence bolt at the A.M.C.'s since the conference bad been in existence. In Lancashire there were a great many small districts in connection with the Order and he considered it would be a good thing 11 they could prevail upon those districts to join Ithe conference. By this means the small districts might be persuaded t• amalgamate and this wsuld be advan- tageous to the Order. Speaking of the proposal to es- tablish a convalescent home in connection with the conference, Isro Gartside said this was rather a large order but he did not see why the conference could not undertake a task even of such magnitude. He believed there was in Lancashire a similar institstion in connec- tion with a portion of the Order of Druids. If it was possible fore section of the Order cf Druids to establish a hems he thought that conference should be able to do the same.
Ero LF.D.HAM (Erbbingten) moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman far his address.

Bro HALEY (Warrington) seconded. He pointed out that the two years during which the conference had been in existence had practically been occupied by the laying down of plant. One object of the conference was consolidation an well as extension. They had in Lanca- shire a great number of districts and it was the object of the conference to make thel:districts more united in their work and to place them on a firmer basis. He felt sure that if they carried en their work with the deter- mination and spirit which they had shown in the past, it would ultimately be crowned with success. The reeelntion was heartily carried, and the CHAIR- MAN responded. The SECRETARY (Bro. C. A. Jones, o! ManeheAer), then presented his annual report, which he regretted was not more favourable. Still when they came to con- eider the suspicion with which the conference was at first looked upon, the difficulties they had to surmount, and the fact that the first twelvemonths was practically occupied by the laying down of the foundation which they bad to work upon, they Gould not expect the Con- ference !o have made a great amount of progress. At the present time the Conference had a membership of , 7,506. The first year it was 7,378. It was to be rsgre- I ted, however, that few of the districts showed progress as far as the initiation of new members was concerned. The distriet of which he was a member,and the majority, lof distriete connected with ths conference seemed to be on the downward grade. Only the Chorley, nandbach, Warrington, and Bebleingten districts, had made pre- geese during the past twelve months. The membership of the Warrington district had during that period inereased from 912 to 943. With regard to the finances of the conference there was a credit balance of £26 13s 9d. In conclusion the secretary urged the import- ance of the work of assieting decaying lodges, and of , profitably investing the funds. He also thought the conference would be doing a good work if they induced email districts to amalgamate. One of the delegates pointed out that the Manchester district was not on the down-grade. It was in a very good position. Bro EDGAR (Warrington) proposel a vote of thanks to the Secretary for Isis report. He said that if they could oily infuse more enthusiasm and more unity into the Order they would make themselves felt. It was ne wonder that Lancashire lodges and districts were going down. What they wanted at the present time was strong sten at the A.M.C. and the Beard of Manay,e- went. Re did not think it was fair and reasonable that practically is dozen men should govern the Order for all time. They could not expect great things in two years. They could not expect to see good fruit during the next two years • They would be thankful if they saw it in five years, and he should be thankful if be could see solidity, unity, friendly spirit, and a general desire to give and take for the purpose of making pro- gress and of making themselves felt. He had en opin- ion that at the present time the A.M.C. and its manage- ment was ten years ahead and it must be dragged back, or else the districts would go down. Bro. ASHCROFT (St. Helens) seconded. With regard to the investments of lodge funds, he thought that if the influential business men in the district would bestir thereselve, they could obtain good, sound investments at a reasonable rate of interest. The resolutien was agreed to.

Bye. W H SUGDEN, Vice. President, of Stalybridge , introduced the subject of " Extension," He was of the opinion that it would be of considerable service if they could get some well-known brethren to visit the die- Mots with a view to opening new lodged or bringing about amalgamations...

After considerable discussion on the subject, the sompany adjourned for tea. After tea, Bro. W H Sudan was elected Preeident and Bro. Lawrence Weir (Warrington) Vice-President. A committee of management was also elected. . . . . . . .

The principal business was to decide who should receive the support of the Conference at the A.M.C. in the election of the various officere. It was resolved to nominate Bro. Gartside for the offiee of Deputy-Chief of the Order, and each district farming the conference will send in nominetirms to that effect. After some polling, Bro Lawrence Weir received the unanimous support of the Conference for a seat on the Board Tot Management,and the districte are pledged to nominate him for that position. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meetine.
The Coroner and the Motor.

Mr. S. Brighouse, Coroner for South-West Lanca- shire, arrived at a Woolton inquest on Monday an hour and a quarter late, and in apologiaing for the delay, be said that. quite recently he had gone in for thallinvention of rho devil, a motor-bicycle. After two or three preliminary runs he thought nobody could teach him anything, and started for Woolton. He did not know whether they knew the nature of the beast, but troubles quickly came. The mixing was 'not right, and when that was remedied a puncture followed, the result being that he had to fall back on a horse to complete the journey.

Six Months Imprionment for Theft of ~,

Horse. At the Liverpool County Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, before Sir W Forwood and ether Innis- trates, William Mackie (28), labourer, pleaded guilty to stealing a mare and bridle and horse cloth- ing, at Warrington, on the 13th July, the property of William Russell, cab proprietor, Bridge-street. Mr Madden, who prosecuted, informed the Bench that prisoner took the horse to Salford, where he tried to sell it As his manner became suspiciene be was arrested, and admitted the theft. Prisoner was sentenced to six months' hard labour. Death of Mrs E. Hatton. _

Many of our r-e—ad—ers will regret to hear of the death of Mrs. Hatton, wife of Mr. Ernest Hatton, of Bewsey OM Farm, Bewsey. The deceased lady, who had been married only abeut four years, was dangbter of Mrs. Reid, of Bewsey Old Hall. She was en a visit to Mrs. Solomon, a married sister, when on Monday evening week she suddenly became ill. Her condition became so grave on the following Thursday that it was deemed necessary to call in three physicians and also to telegraph to Warrington for her husband. Notwithstanding all medical attention she became worse, and expired on Saturday afternoon last at 3 30. Much sympathy has been extended to the husband in his sudden bereavement. The funeral took place at St. Paul'i Church, Warrington, an Wednesday afternoon.
Will of the Late Captain H. R. D'A., Willis.

Captain Henry Rudolph D'Anvers Willis, of Bala- need Hall, Present, Lancashire, J.P., and DL.. Lord of the Manor of Wl•iston, who died on the 13th or August last, aged 68 years, son of the late Idr D'A Willis, of Haloneed, appointed as executors of his will of the 17th July; 1899, Captain Charles Bean. mount D'Anyere Willis, of 4, Summer-place, and Mr Arthur Richmond Ferrer, solicitor, to each of whom the testator bequeathed £100; and he bequeathed to the trustees of the marriage se:.tletnent of his daughter Georgina, wife of Mr Henry Arthur Levison Yemen, £2,000, or such smaller sum as will make up her perti_.n to £10,000; and he bequeathed to the trustees of the marriage settlements of his daughter Cecilia, wife of Mr James Binney, such sum as will make up her portion to £10,000; and bequeathed to his wife, Mrs Alice Willis. daughter of the Rev It Hornby, of Lythwond Hall,Salop, .£l,OOO, his horses and carriages, and he charged his real estate with an annuity for her of £BOO. He settled all of his real estate and his leasehold and copvhold estate in favour of his son,Richard Atherton D'Anyers Willie, and his issue, male and general,with the remainder to the issue of his eaughters, and it is made con- ditional that each tenant for life shall use the name of Willis and quarter the arms of Willis of Hale. need. Captain Willis made heirlooms of the effects at Halanead Hall, and be left his residuary estate in trust as if it were money arising from the sale of settled real estate under the Settled Lamle Act. The testator's estate has been valued at £159,855 12s 3cl gross. including personalty!of the net value of X 77,83,1 14s 4d.

div.head: ILLUSTRATED FASHICWS.
div.p: ILLUSTRATED FASHICWS.

Furs naturally merit much attention at this season of the year when they form some of the most comfortable items of dress. Of course every one who can possibly do so should avoid all imitation furs, as these do not wear long and the dyes employed are apt to come off and soil any delicate coloured blouse or coat. But i nevertheless those whose dress allowance is not 'I sufficiently elastic to stretch to the luxury of a really good necklet or coat can with care find almost its equivalent in one of the cheaper form of skins which has been dressed and dyed to an exceedingly good imitation of the real article. Fashion having set its approval on basques as a necessary feature of the newest coats, smooth furs have advanced in popularity and among these grey squirrel, golden beaver and moleskin rank as first favourites.

A most comfortable coat of the three-quarter variety is sketched, of which fur is a promi- nent feature. In this instance the coat is worn as an evening wrap and is made of an artistic tone of green velvet, the fur being white fox. It is arranged in the form of a very deep collar or cape caught in front by two sets of ornamental clasps, with a couple of long ends at either side depending tb the hems of the jacket. The cuffs are deep and loose, as fashion

div.head: COMFORTABLE WRAP.
div.p: A COMFORTABLE WRAP.

and comfort are unanimous on this point foi all garments of this description. A coat could be made in this style of some other material which would permit of wear in the day-time. For instance, black velvet or silk, or even a smooth-surfaced cloth of good quality would look &ell with an astrachan collar and cuffs, while grey chinchilla would make an even more effective trimming. All the latest tippets and collars of fur are very deep, coming well over the shoulders, while pelerines and stole-shaped boas with flat ends reaching beyond the knees are much in evide.nep, and have successfully ousted from popular estimation the collarettes fashioned in the form of some animal which have been se much worn for the last two or three winter seasons. Muffs are large, and some of the best and most fashionable specimens have a cluster of tails, or the head and paws fixed in the centre. This mode offers an excellent oppor- tunity for concealing any worn parts in our last season's muff by the addition of a few tails, • the cost being inconsiderable.

Very smart, and particularly up-to-date is the little coat sketched, whose cut and style is simple yet stylish. The collarless coat is quite the thing this winter, while stitched etrappings and the finish given by a twist of cord and a tassel is a distinct novelty. This coat can be worn open or closed, and is a good example of the " tailor-made" proper, the
A SMART COAT.

sleeves being cut in the correct "coat sleete style. It could be made to match the skirt, or in black or fawn cloth ;to wear with anything, as is most suitable. In either case a bright red or green silk lining wottici look well when the coat is worn open. Tartan also is effective, but in every case the fronts must be silk lined, even if a cheaper lining is used for the rest of the coat.

It is in our sleeves that fashion is evincing most of its vagaries, and some of the varieties are picturesque almost to an extreme. It is not given to every woman to be picturesque, and, the tailor-made girl should avoid all efforts in this direction, as the result will be only ludicrous and anything but becoming. The kimono sleeve is the favourite for out-of-door wraps, but the latest style is the old-fashioned leg-o -mutton with the fulness increasing from the elbow to the wrist, where it is shaped back again into a pointed cuff which comes over the back of the hand.

The blouse depicted is suitable for after- noon house wear, and is made of cream- coloured viyella tucked in regular lines at intervals, and boasts a deep collar of silk to match trimmed with lace insertions and applique Qf a dull yellr ^ A pale green silk bow

div.head: AFTERNOON BLOUSE.
div.p: AFTERNOON BLOUSE.

aid ends finish the front and is made detachable so that the coloar may be varied at will. TheA little collar and front are of tucked silk, un- lined, and could also be made detachable, so that lace or some similar transparent material could be substituted for evening wear. Blouw, and bodices are very difficult to distinguish froth each other, as there is little difference between the two, but to my mind I always imagine that an unlined garment may be termed a blouse. and the more closely fitting lined arrangement a bodice. anyhow "what's in a name ? " and whether the blouse may be submerged into the bodice as was often foretold, or not, is al matter of indifference so long as we meet with dainty and becoming modes, and this season there is no fear of us suffering from any lack of these. COQUETTE.

div.head: "AS YOU LIKE IT!"
div.p: "AS YOU LIKE IT!"

Mr T Courtneidge's famous production of " As You Like It" has still another week to run at tie Prince's Theatre, Manchester, so that the oppor- tunity still remains for those who have not yet seen it,ts do so. We strongly advise all lovers of a goad hing in theatrical matters not te miss the chance for, surely, Sbakeepear's pastoral comedy was never produced in richer style and to the accompaniment of better acting than it is at the Prince's Theatre. Enough has been said and written during the run of the piece to familiar- ise all theatregoers and newspaper readers with its many excellencies. Mr William Archer, one of the severest aid most exacting of London critics, made a special visit to Manchester to see " As you like it 'and was well pleased, while it is doubtful if there has yet been a visitor to the Theatre since the inception of the comedy who has not been de- lighted with the performance, unless be lacked the , capacity to appreciate anything of a higher class than pantomime. The company is an exceptionally' strong one, and the level excellence of tie acting, even in the minor parts, has much to do with the unqualified satisfaction expressed by each large audience. Some of the scenes are so well pour- trayed and the Shakeqpearien atmosphere and sentiment so cleverly suggested that one would willingly encore them individually if such a thing were permissible. Miss Nora Kerin, Miss Jenny Buckle, Mr Courtice Pounds, Mr Rol- break Blinn, 'Mr Gerald Lawrence Wand Mr B Clarence are all splendid in the leading parts and fully merit the warm recognition which it is their nightly lot to receive. The staging of the piece, too, is wonderfully done, some of the scenes in the forest of Arden by Conrad Trif'Qr.l•r and Hawes Craven being superb examples of scene-painting.

But,enough! "As you like it" mast be seen to be appreciated, and we hope those of our readers who have not yet been, will take an early opportunity of visiting the Prince's Theatre ere the curtain drops for the last time on this charming comedy.

Accident in a Railway Shed. On Saturday evening James Whitworth (33), of Lengshaw-street, was admitted to the Infirmary suffering from a broken leg, caused by a fall in one of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's sheds at Bank Quay. Temporary Authority. At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday Mrs Priscilla Newall was granted temporary. authority to sell at the Mulberry Tree, Stockton Heath,in lieu of her late husband.

Local Oddfellowship. On Saturday evening a smoking concert was held at the Blue Lion, Market-place, to celebrate the anniversary of the Loyal Garibaldi Lodge of tbe National Independent Order of Oddfellows. Among those present were :—Rro James Branch all, Grand Master; Bro W Duncan, Deputy Grand Master; Bro J Smith, D.T. Daring the evening PP G William Hill made a presentation to the Lodge Treasurer, Br° James Smith, f-r 25 years' service of a silver-mounted walking-stick and smoker's corn- panien.—The NG, Bro R Blacki,haw, who was supported by the Secretary, Bro S Dickiugen, and PP G k Edwin E Pester. requested PPG M William Hill to make the presentation.—Bro Hill spoke highly of Bro Smith's services, and Bro Thomas F Nevins,PP 0 M Pester and the Secretary endorsed all that he had said.—ln responding, Bro Smith Said ha was pleased that he was so much respected, and its value to him was more than trebled by the manner in which it had been pre- sented. Songs were given by Bros James La, Jolley, Daniels. Blacksbaw, William Hands, Mc- Donald and Platt; Bro Bates contributed violin solos, and Bro Thomas Knight recited.

Farm Fire at Whitley. A serious fire broke out az: the farm of Mr Leach, Lower Whitley, on Monday afternoon. Informa- tion was telegraphed to the Warrington Fire Engine Station and Superintendent Turner, and a full com- plement of men,with the steam fire engine "Mal.or," turned out, Upon arrival at Whitley they found a large shippon 40 yards by 10 yards, in filmes. The building contained about 200 boxes of potato setts and a large quantity of seed and other farm pro- duce. A good supply of water was obtained from a brook 350 yards away, and the engine was got to work with twe powerful sets. Fortunately the wind was not blowing in the direction of the stacks of produce in the yard, and the brigade were successful in saving the cartshed and a quantity of oilcake and other produce. 'I he other portions of the buildings and contents were, however, totally destroyed. The owner of the property is Sir George Chetwode, Bart. The estimated damage to stock and property is about £7OO. The brigade arrived back at Warrington at 10 55 p m.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

A WARRINGTON BUTCHER HEAVILY NINRD-BISEASED MEAT A fine of £lO and costs was imposed upon Thomas Everett butcher, of Crossley-street, at the Warrington Police Court on Monday. The charge preferred against him wae that of having in Ms possession diseased reeas which was intended 'for human consumption on October 17th.-Mr Stanley Wil- son, Deputy Town Clerk,prosecuted, and stated that certain information was received by the Health Department some days prior to the date on which the meat wee seized, that a cow belonging to Mr Thomas Kilshaw, farmer, Sankey. had been ailing for some time. At 5 a.m. on October 17th Inepeetor Flood went on duty in Liverpool-road. At about 7.be he met the defend- ant's trap coming from the direction of Sankey. He stopped it and asked the driver-a man named Jackson- what he had got there The reply was Some beef." The Inspector turned over the cover to look at it, and asked Jackson if he had the internal organs [Another man in the trap,who was in the employ of the defendant, said" We have not got them." The trap was driven on, and the Inspector immediately went to the defendant's premises in Crossley-street. He saw the meat which had not been taken out of the trap found it to coseist of two bind quarters and two fore quarters, properly dressed, and the head, liver, heart and kidneys of a cow. He made a thorough examination of the meat and found a large tubercle in the centre of the liver, and a cluster of tubercles at the side of the throat, The defendant was pre. sent during the examination,and in answer to the Inspector's request for the internal organs he said "I don't know any- thing about them. My man who"dreseed it has not arrived yet." The man in question shortly afterwards came up, and on being asked a similar question, said the lungs were full of cold and he threw them away. The Inspector said he would seize the meat as being unfit for human food, and defendant remarked " I suppose I shall get into trouble for this. lam sorry I had anything to do with it. If they send me to prison I shall be ruined," The meat was then taken to the Town Hall, and the Inspector obtained a con- veyance and went to Sankey. After having a conversation with Mr Kilshaw, he got a fork and dug up the internal organs from a midden where they had been buried. It was found that both lungs were affected with tubercles, and they were black in places and consolidated as a result of a severe attack of pneumonia. The lungs were inspected by the Medical Officer. who certified the whole of the meat as unfit for food, and an order was obtained for its destruction. One would have thought that a man of such long experi- ence in the trade as Mr Everett, as a prudent man, would have made inquiries before sending the men to the farm. It was a very serious case indeed- Arthur Kilshaw, son of Thomas Kilshaw, Whittle Hall Farm, Sankey, said his father sent hint to the defendant's premises on October 16th. He was told to ask alir Everett if he would come and look at the cow as soon as possible as his (witness's) father was going away. Witness knew the cow had been ill. He saw the defendant who told one of his men to go and look at the cow. The man went back with witness and the Sow was killed and dreseed•-Inspeeter Flood corroborated Mr Wilson's statement.-In answer to the defendant he said he did not find anything wrong with the meat without care- ful examination.-Mr Wilson: But an experienced butcher would have no difficulty in finding it,-Dr Gornall said the carcase was that of a beast deficient in fat. The meat was of a dark colour and not setting well. Its condition was Corn- patible Wad wlthone would expect as the result of a lingering illness. In the lungs there were numerous tubtroles of a comparatively advanced nature,and probably of some menthe standing. There were also signs of acutelpneumaaia of More recent origin. There were tubercles on the windpipe,and the intestines were also affected. The carcase generally he con- demned as anfit for human food.-Defendant stated that he had not examined the beast before Mr Flood came and clicl not know there was anything wrong with it.-4 -Mr Browne,who watched the case on behalf of Mr Kilehaw, said his client knew the cow was suffering from gargle and inflammation of the udder. He said he would have someone to see the animal and if it was fit to be killed and used for human food it could be destroyed. He sent for Mr Everett to come and see the beast and the latter sent two of his men. Mr Kilshaw was not there at the time, having gone to a sale, and never sold the cow to Mr Everett at all. The men killed and dressed the beast without a purchase having been made. Neither the farmer nor the butcher could possibly tell there was anything wrong with the beast until it was being dress- ed.-The Beneh considered their decision in private, and on their return the Chairman said they thought the case had been fully proved, and they intended to put a stop to the practice. Defendant would be fined £lO and costs (Ell 10 in alit, or, in default of payment, two months' imprisonment.

div.head: MINOR OASES.
div.p: MINOR OASES.
Warrington Borough Court.

MONDAY.—Before Mr F Monks an the chair), Councillor Smethurst, and Messrs Birchen, Wright and Thornton. MINOR Smith, 5, Erwood-street, and Patrick Gray,23, Bank-street. were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Erwood-street on the 13th October and were bound over to keep the peace for six months. Smith, who was the aggressor, to pay the costs.— For a similar offence in Btlekley-street, James Leg's, 15. Bowes-street, and John Fell, 2, Dolan's-yard, were bound over and ordered to pay the costs, 5s each.—Harry Carlisle, 51, Rolleston-street, was fined 5s for not having a lighted lamp attached to his vehicle in Foundry-street, on October 19th. A TRAM CONDUCTOR ASSAULTED.—Christophor Pritehards, 19 Barnard-street, was summoned for assaulting Joseph Knox, a tram-conclactor, OH October 15. He pleaded not guilty. Mr Stanley Wilson, who prosecnteduaid the defend- ant and another man were on the top of a car which left Rylands-street at 945 p.m. and Knox went for their fares. The other man was paying 2d for the two, but before he put It into the guard's hands, he dropped a penny. A search was made for the coin but in vain, and the other man offers ito pay the other penny. Defendant refused to let the other man pay the money and would not pay it himself. He struck and kicked Knox, and the car had to be stopped so that the men could hi separated.—The defendant alleged that the guard dropped the penny, and wonld not allow hint to leave the ear, and that was the reason of the souffle.—A fine of lOs and cost (£l. 1s) was indicted the Chairman re- arking that if people were to be allowed to do that kind of m,ing the care would simply become places of rowdyism.

div.head: GOOD 1 EMPLARS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: GOOD 1 EMPLARS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLESTOWN.

A tea party and concert in celebration of the 30th anniversary of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday even:ng. There was a fair number to tea, at the close of which a concert was given.the Rev G Cook presiding. An address was given by Bro Morris Jones, district I secretary. The musical programme embraced a solo "By the Fountain " Mrs Williams; solo " The Holy City" Master Harold Roberts ; solo "Fiddle and I," Miss Stronach ;recitation "The Fence and the Ambulance" Miss B Smith ; solo, Mr J Griffin t solo " Killarney " Master Harold Roberts ; gramophone selections Mr Joseph Smith: solo " The Carnival " Miss M Stronach ; Lancashire reading, Mr John Warburton ; solo " In the Golden Eventide " Mrs Williams ; recitetion " Beet- hoven's Moonlight Sonata ': Miss B Smith. Solo " Let Brotherly love continue" Mr A Grissold. Bro George Clarke in his report said that the Order of Good Tempters which originated in New York State United States eq/kmerican in 1851 celebrated its Jubilee during last year by an energetic crusade for the exten- sion of the order throuehout the world, resulting in the institution of hundreds of new lodges and the admission of many thousands of new members. In our own country,there was an average of one new Branch opened for every day in the year. It is calculated that there are over 10,000 branches with about 600,000 members, and in Earlestown there is just a small company, a unit in this vast army, tbe greatest temperance organi- zation in the country. Our report in tee Exeter Grand Lodge Session during Easter last showed that there were in this country 2,200 adult and juvenile branches with nearly 114.000 members, being an increase on tlae year of about 250 branches and 13,000 inemtbers. In our own district of South-West Lanessnire we have about 43,000 members. eur Hope of Earlestown Lodge was started 30 years ago by a few friends—men and women—in an upper room in Market-street,where nearly two years were well Spent in laying the foundation for future service ; the Lodge removing in August 1874 to another upper room in Bridge-street, where a vary useful work was carried on for about 17 years, when circumstances led to another change in the meeting place, to the present room on these premises. During the put 30 years the Lodge has had a varied career, at times our numbers leave been comparatively nmall,searcely sufficient attend- ing to fill the various offices and carry on the good work, however changes came about, better times were experi- enced and during ens particular year over 140 candi- dates and our progress seemed to be phenomenal. It is calculated that during the life time of the Lodge ; more than 1,100 persons men and women have been admitted and yet to-day there is not a membership in good standing of three figures. On Sunday, Bro J A Lee of Liverpool preached a couple of temperance sermons in tie Primitive Metho- dist Shape!.

ndependent Order of Rechabites —Warrington District No. 4, The quarterly meeting of the above district was held on Saturday in the Temperance Mission Hall, Latchford. The average age of the members is 28 years. A plan el tents visiting committee was presented and adopted. Bro Wright,J D BE, presented his quarteriy report. There were 13 juvenile branches in the district with a membership of 546 this giving an increase of 16 members during the quarter and six juveniles having been transferred to the adult ' t'ants. It was deeided to accept the invitation to "old the next district meeting at Ashton, this being .e Iniisi uilann4.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP.
CHESHIRE V. LANCASHIRE. THE HOLDER! OVERPLLYED.

The above ins telt was played on the irwell-lane Enclosure, Runcorn, on Saturday. The weather fortunately was all that could be desired and with the exception o a slight breeze, hardly sufficient to interfere with good football, the climatic conditions were exceptionally good. As might he expected there was one of the largest crowds -ver seen at the head- quarters of the" Myrtle Green "and there would be fully firs thousand present when the turn stiles had finished reoording. Both teams co-aid be well considered to be fairly represented. On the Lancashire side there were two changes Harris taking the place of Hogg in the threequarter line and G Boardman taking the place of A S Boarder oa. Cheshire turned out as selected. The following are the teams :- Lancashire.—Smith (Salford), back ; Harris (Warrington). Wilson (Broughton Rangers). clptain,n Valentine (Swinton). and Fish (Warrington). three-quarter backs : W James and James (Broughton Rangers) half backs ; Tunney, Rhspps, and Heath (Salford), Ferguson and Fraser (Oldhena), Board- man (Leigh), Evans (Swinton). and Cram (Brenghton Rangers), forwards. .-.Theshire, —Boughton (Runcorn). captain, hack ; Jones. Butterworth; and Warder (Runcorn), and Hodgson (Stock• port) three-quarter backs ; Richardson (Runcorn) and Booth (Stockport), half backs ; Walker. Williams. Wools. Moulton., Farmer, and Tomlinson (Runcorn) Foster (Stockport), and Brown (Birkenhead), forwards. Referee. Mr W Robinson (Yorkshire) ; touch judges, Mr G Robinson (ehefilaire), and Mr J. H Smith (Lancashire). Lancashire were fortunate in winning the toss. Cheshire having M play with a strong son in their eyes. Farmer started. Wilson returning, play settling down in the Cheshire territory. d break away initiated by Richardson was smartly frustrated by W James, Valentine afterwards marking and placing Cheshire on the defensive. Houghton relieved, finding tonoh, but a penalty kick taken by Valentine regained the ground lest. Cheshire at this stage were rather more than holding their own, lack of combination placing Lancashire at a deeded disadvantage. The first brilliant bit of play was seen when Jones. picking smartly from the serum broke away with a fine sprint. slipping down with only Smith to elude. • free kick again gave Lancashire a chance but they mad little of it. A moment later Fish with a splendid run and Cross kick took the play on the Cheshire line ighton Clearing finely after a partioularly fierce attack. A Smart for- ward dribble initiated by Walker conveyed the leather to the Lancashire 25 and it really seemed that Cheshire had the Red Rose line at their mercy but Smith cleared in the nick of time. Very quickly the leather was again in motion Fisk getting in one of his dangerous sprints. For feet up Cheshire were penalized, W James missing the sticks by inches. Another particularly fierce onslaught saw the Cheshire quarters again invaded, Fish eventually touching down after offside play. The red and white hoops still maintaine 1 the upper hand, a nasty fumble by Warder letting Lancashire in. Danger was averted for the moment but the strongest defence could not have withstood such a terrific fusilade. The first points came to Lancashire as the result of very smart p lay. Gathering finely the brothers James indulged in a particularly choice bit of work after which wile= had but little difficulty in grounding at the corner. WlJames made a very good attempt to convert but failed. This portion of the game saw the Cheshire nushers losing the ball repeatedly in the serum and but for the excellent defensive work of the backs the Cheese C senty must have been severely handled. By dint of hard play, howeve-, Cheshire worked the leather into their opponents quarters, but a series of penalties made the home County lose more ground. On two occasions Booth, for Chsshire, had the chance of getting the rear division in motion, but chose to kick wildly to his opponents. Harris from a packion the line nearly did the trick, but Houghton upset him at the critical moment. Pressure still came I ront the Lancashire team, and Houghton was called upon repeat- edly to save. At length W James merle a grand opening which should have tel to points, but Valentine, who was playing anything but a brilliant game, missed a pass. The second point was not, however, long in coming. By a series ' of scrums and penalties the leather was taken to the Cheshire line, where from the scrum W James gathered, and running round the pack easily eluded Houghton. Half-time came immediately after with Lancashire leading by one goal, two tries, to Cheshire nil. i4The change of ends again saw Lane tense on the aggressive Jones stopping a determined rush In time. W James, how- ever, again -et the rear division to work, Fish nearly ground- ing at the corner. Playing with a little more spitit,Cheshire managed to forge ahead hut Wilson nyking a fine opening again transferred play to the Cheshire 25. For the first time the game developed an exciting if not an interest- I lug phase. There was much give and take play in which Fish, Valentine. Wilson, and the brothers James played a prominent parties break-away initiated by Jones placed Lan- cashire on the defe use for a moment,but the ball was quickly taken back. Cheshire, though, were net to be dented. doses, who had played a grand game. throughout. gathered from Booth. and sheering thr 'ugh his opponents was grandly taskied on the line by Valentine and held But with the goal in sight the Cheshire lads made a spasmodic effort whichresalt- ed in Hodgson touching at the corner, Farms failing at goal. It only took Lancashire a i'ew moments to wipe Out the slight stain. A passing movement between 8 James, W James, Valentine and Wilson enabled the latter to mere at the cor- ner when every one thonght the ball was lost, James made a poor effort to convert. Oheshire were still forced to defend, Booth with bad putting in the scrum losing Cheshi re a lot of ground. At this stage the game degenerated into an ex- hibition of penalty kicks. The play at length opened out with a fine run from Fish who transfesed the game from mid- field to his opponents gut!, fro ighton earns to the rescue, play settling at midfield. A grand roinldned movern ent was neatly frustrated by F Forster who grassed Valentine in fint class style Give and take play followed 0 the finish Lanca- shire easily holding the upper hand. Final : —Laneashlre, one goal, three tries ; Cheshire one try.

div.head: 7iattero to the Ebitor
div.p: 7iattero to the Ebitor
Mr. Dodds and Pearson and Knowles Limited.

Sir,-.4 hardly think it necessary, but I may say that I am not a shareholder in the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., htd., nor in any company or firm which is doing or has done business with the Warrington Corporaticin. I am, yours truly, JAMES DODDS. Bews.y-road, 24th October. 1902. The Conservative Assoc!ation and St. Austin's Ward.

-- Si,-4e the President of the Conservative Association made some references that I consider unfair both to my- self personally, an i to my candidature for St. Austin'e Ward in the Cooservative interest at the forthcoming municipal elections, I trust that, in common fairness. You will give to a reply from ine the same publicity as has been given to the attack upon me by Mr John , Fortunately for me, Mr Wnite's own words expose his motiYNi so clearly that I might leave the following quotation from his speech on Tuesday evening last, without comment, to the impartial judg- ment of any intelligent man. Referring to me he said That gentleman name to him a month ago, and toll him that he was in a position to become a candidate for St Austin's Ward. Ile (the chairman) did not know Mr Lord. He had never seen him or heard of him ; but if he had been a prominent Coaservative he should have heard of him. B had his doubts about him and accordingly decided to make inquiries, and told him to come again in a week. He made in- quiries from three differeot sources, and was told twit Mr Lord was a Radical." That a man who had never seen me or heard of we before should " have his doubts" as to whether I $.4 aa a Conservative will strike most people as very pecodar. That being so, it is not surprising that the useful, and, in the circum- stances, highly desirable evidence that I was a Radical was obtained from " three different and independent sources "its th 3 nick of time. I had already been adopted unanimously by the Con- servative Ward Committee of Sc Austin's, and was not allowed to be present while theie charges of dishonour and hypocrisy were made against ma on the taro word of three individuals who dare not accuse me openly, but who did not think it beneath them to give me a stab in the dark. Why was I not brought face to face with my accusCrs ? I had reason to believe that Mr Tinaion was one of the " three different independent sources " from which evidenco of my Radicalism was obtained, and, in con- sequence, addressed to him the following letter, which was7delivered to him by my assistant, Mr Lightfoot. 128 Bridge-street. Warrington. 20th October. 1902, "To David Tinnion, Esq.. 18 Winmarleigh-street. Dear sir,—As there is a statement in. circulation and attributed to you, t, the effect that I am a Liberal, and was an active worker in your support at a former municipal election, I shall be much obliged if you will 4reply by return either admitting or repudiating the Manthorship of the statement referred to. It is unnecessary for me to add that the words attri- buted to you have not the shadow of a foundation in fact.
1 am, dear sir, yours faithfully, JOHN LORD.

When Mr Tinnion had perused my letter he could not conceal his agitation and was just able to gasp, "TEN Mr Lord that I am not entering into any correspondence with him, and all that I know is that :le voted strongly for me six years ago ; but he is not voting for me this time, because the Conservatives are putting him up, and paying his expenses." These are Mr Tinnion's words reduced to writing., on the spot, by Mr Lightfoot. I consider ii clear that Mr Tinnion betrayed his connection , with the "three different and independent soutees " so useful to Mr White. That a political opponent like Mr Tinnion should be consulted, by the President of the Conserva- tive Association, as to the sincerity of my or any other body's Conservatism might seem strange if we could not connect cause with effect:

But I have beets accused of attempting to use the Conservative Association to further the interests of the " Municipal Non-Trading Committee." Admitted ! I see no harm in that. I will use every means in my power to stamp out municipal corruption ; and, there- tore, I would very gladly have accepted the support of the Conservative Association as an additional weapon in what lam convinced is a just and righteous cause ; and it is well to remember that although my nomination as the official Conservative candi- date for St. Austin's Ward was rejected by 37 votes to 5, there were 163 members present, and that the abstention of 121 was an eloquent protest against proceedings that will appear all tee more unjustifiable the loager they are subjected to sober and unprejudiced reflection.
I have never been a Liberal. I have never been a member of any Liberal organization. I have always been a Conservative and I am still a member of the Warrington Conservativ e Club. I have

div.head: SHORTNESS OF BREATH.
div.p: SHORTNESS OF BREATH.

Shortness of breath is a very common trouble from which many suffer. They cannot move quickly without discomfort ; ordinary exertion such as a hasty move- ment, or the climoing of stairs, gives them naokt dis- tressing discomfort. Many fail to connect this symptom with the kidneys, and yet there is no doubt that in thousands of cases it is due to failing kidney power. Mr C Gamey, of Kidrnere, Barn Green, Coshana, writing on May 30, 1902, gives an interesting experi- ence. He suffered from severe backache, pain at the Fide, and shortness of breath. Sometimes be felt so bad he did not know what to do. We condition was welt that he could hardly keep to his work. Relief only came with Dedd's Kidney Pills. " I can say," he writes, "Dodd's Kidney Pills have entirely cured me; my broathing is all right, and I can work as well as ever." Dodd's Kidney Pills, have cured thousands of such cases. They cure the kidneys, and well kidneys make pure blood; the result is that distressing symptoms of heart trouble disappear when the strain is removed trom that over-worked organ. Hunting Accident near Whitey. On Thursday of last week, Mr P N Avery, of Grappenhall, met with an accident while cub-hunt- ing with the North Cheshire hounds near the Black Jane Farm, near Whitley, occupied by Mr Wilkin- son. He was taken home in a conveyance lent by Mr Wilkinson, and remained unconscious until Monday, suffering from concussion of the brain and a fractured rib. Is is now progressing favourably, The Estates of the Late Messrs. R. Davies and Sylvanus Chandley. Reber% Davies, of Birchdale, Warrington, and of Chester, solieitor, £86,348. Alderman Sy',anus Chandley, 77, of dews Henry and Syvanus Chand- bov. of Warrington, Mayor of Warrington, 1874, £16,039.

A Corporal in the 2nd Battalion Scottish Rifies,named Patrick Bonel, jumped from a Midland passenger train between Cudworth and Normsnton last night, and sus- tained a fraction of the skull and other injuries. He is a married man, and had been away from home about three years. His brother met him at Birmingham and communicated news of some private affliction which greatly depressed the homo-comer. Mr Joseph Carter, of the Blue Barrel Inn, Elland has issued a notice that in future his licensed house will close at 10 p m each day, instead of 11 o'clock, as at present. For some time Mr Carter has closed lois house entirely on Sundays. It is believed his present step will be followed by several of his competitors. Suspense concerning Miss Annie Wilcock. daughter of Mr William Wlllcock, architect,Moorhead Villas,Shinley, who has been missing from home since October 21st, was terminated yesterday, but by a very painful dis- covery. Two Keighley men, named Turner and Alfred Naylor, walking along the canal bank at Saltaire, saw the body of a young woman in the water near to the Hirst Locks. Me body was taken out of the water,and afterwards identified as that of the missing lady.

div.head: ROYAL PROGRESS.
div.p: THE ROYAL PROGRESS.
THE KING AND QUEEN LEAVING BUCKINGHAM PALACE.

Never has any Royal pageant gone off more successfully than the King's progress through London last Saturday: and everything combined to make it a great and gorgeous success. "I am so very glad that it is a fine day for all of us," saidihis Majesty in accepting the London County Council's address in Trafalgar Square: and, despite the threatening aspect during the early hours, the weather was splendid. However, the order had gone out from headquarters during the doubtful outlook for all the troops to wear their heavy military coats and cloaks; and the only splashes of colour in a grey picture were lent by the House- hold Cavalry and the Yeomen of the Guard. The whole programme went off like clockwork, and not the slightest hitch occurred, except the loss of the Lord Mayor's three-cornered hat, which was dropped at Temple Bar, but sent on after him by a mounted messenger. Punctuality wee adhered to all along the route: and the scheduled times worked out woAderfully well. At noon the great pageant, tEe most extensive since the Diamond Jubilee, started from Buckingham Palace, and proceeded amidst terrific cheering along its first stage to the L.C.C, stand in Trafalgar Square rid the Mall and Pall Mall. At the great stand, which has become quite a familiar feature of the square during the last few months, Sir

John McDougall, asthairman of the Council, pre- sented an address from the Central Municipal Authority, to which the King replied most graciously. Amongst others in the front row of the stand at the three Boer generals, Botha, Delarey, and De Wet—who were present at the King's and their own desire by special invitation. The procession proceeded by Duncannon Street into the Strand, where at a crimson-coloured dais between St. Clement Danes and St. Mary-le-Strand Churches two more loyal addresses,—one from the City of Westminster and the other from the four- teen boroughs in the north of London,—were presented and graciously accepted, his Majesty in each case making a well-turned little speech. At Temple Bar the Lord May or was waiting on foot and, as Chief Magistrate of the City, proffered the King the pearl sword with a humble obeisance, following the medimval custom. Upon its return he mounted his horse and rode at the lead of his Majesty's personal escort to the Guildhall. Here all the guests were in readiness, and their Majesties were immediately escorted to their canopied throne on the dais, where the Recorder read the City's loyal address of welcome, to which the King replied appropriately before taking his seat. At the head table was seated a notable gathering of me-

iseour ef the king's visit. Here, too, the decors- tient; were very fine; and Southwark was entered under a most notable arch. In front of the Council Hall of the borough a pavilion of purple and gold had been erected, and here a loyal address was presented by the Mayor of Southwark, hi conjunction with the Mayors of Deptford, Lambeth, Wandsworth, Bermondsey, Lewisham, Greenwich and Woolwich—Battersea being un- pleasantly conspicuous by its official absence. This called forth a wild burst of enthusia.m which ob- viously delighted the King and Queen who were markedy gracious in their reception of the greetings of their poorer subjects. The procession then con- tinued its progress, recrossing the river by West- minster Briage. and passing up densely packed
THROUGH LUDGATX

Whitehall, and, rid the Mall, back to the Palace, which was reached at half-past three, the approxi- mately scheduled time. The Royal progross must be pronounced an un- qualified success : and their Majesties must, indeed, be gratified at the enthusiasm their prescgace calls forth from their most loyal subjects. The King, in a heavy cloak over his Field-marshal's uniform, look conspicuously well and radiantly happy : and was obvious that he was delighted with every- thing, and not least the marvellous enthusiasm on he South side of the river, where the assembled crowds bore themselves with an air of feeling that ihis was -their special procession, organised in printis on their behalf. His Majesty's speeches in reply to the various addresses were most happy and cordial : and he seemed genuinely touched at the frequent references to his dangerous illness.,

THE LORD MAYOR, SIR JOSEPH DIMSDALE, AND MAJOR-GENERAL SIR HENRY TROTTER, WHO STAGE-MANAGED THE PROCEEDINGS. The Queen, the idol of the people's hearts, never looked more lovely; and a full half of the reception was directed personally to her. Queen Alexandra was dressed in orange coloured tints and furs, and smiled and bowed most graciously the whole time. Sunday, which recalled the great Thanksgiving Service of thirty years ago, was not so fine un- fortunately: but, needless to say, not a corner or a cranny in St. Paul's Cathedral was not filled to repletion : and none who were present will ever forget the solemnity of the occasion, and the whole service was most impressive. Their Majesties, however, despite the inclemency of the weather, did not disappoint their loyal sub- jects, who agXin turned out in large and enthusi- astic crowds. Driving by the Embankment, the King, as on the day before, accepted and returned the City's sword to the Lord Mayor: and St. Paul's was reached punctually. The aisle VMS lined by the Honourable Artillery Com he Queen sat in

THEIR MSJESTIES IN ST. PAUL'S ON SUNDAY. (By Oar Own Special Arti4.) specially prepared stalls under a canopy. The service was conducted by the Bishops of London and Stepney, assisted by the Dean and Chapter of the Cathedral: and the first named preadied a most appropriate sermon on Psalm cavil, 11 and 12— "God spake once, and twice have I heard the same, the power that belongeth unto God: but thou, Lord, art merciful." The service throughout was MOSt fervently followed on all sides. At its conclusion their Majesties drove baek to Buckingham Palace, this • time by Newgate Street, Cheapside and Oxford Street: and again their reception Ivas moat vinthusiastie and heartfelt

the Royal Family, who had been most enthusias- tically received all along the route, with the Prince of Wales, who rode beside his Royal father's carriage, on the Queen's immediate left The guests at the luncheon, which in accordance with City custom, was cold, made a most distinguished gathering, including Cabinet ministers, foreign ambassadors, judges, Privy Councillors, and all the leading men of the day. At the conclusion of the banquet, which lasted less than an hour, the Common Crier, Major Ker• Fox, gave the toast oi "ilk Majesty the King," which was most enthuginstically received, the first verse of the National Anthem being sung, led by Madame Albani. Then followed the toasts of "The Queen and , the Royal Family," and "The Lord Mayor and Prosperity to the City a London," toth of which were most cordially honoured. After luncheon their Majesties retired to specially fitted-up withdrawing rooms, which had been arranged as a surprise and delighted the City's great guests. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCIOBBR 31st 1902

IF the dominant Im- An Imperial Failure. penal sentiment of the day were really a passion to govern justly and well, to use the gifts of com- mand which we suppose ourselves to possess in a high degree for the benefit of the odd assortment of alien races under our sway, the events of the past two weeks would have afflicted the nation profoundly. For once more the dismal failure of our administration in Ireland has been exposed. The vulgar Imperialist is doubtless unmoved. His aim is conquest and his distraction warfare. He

follows an Indian froutior campaign by the help of the illustrated papers with the utmost zest. He remembers all about the storming of the heights of Dargai, but he does not know that India is now passing through a fourth consecutive year of famine. Since the battle of Omdurman he has never once .3ast a thought to the Soudan, and even South Africa is rapidly ceasing to interest him. This numerous class of persons will feel no shame at the present state of Ireland. And yet the revelations which Mr O'BRIEN has dragged to the light go to the very root of our administra- tion. No one imagines that Irishmen love our rule; no one fancies that it is particularly mild : no one supposes that it has built up a prosperous people; and everyone is more or less aware that the population of Ireland has dwindled by half, while that of the United Kingdom has nearly doubled. But there is a sort of superstition that if we are severe we are also just. We may take care to appoint four Protestant magistrates to one Catholic, but the theory is that they are impar- tial. The world is not made like that. You can not govern a people against its will without resort- ing to what are called exceptional measures. You cannot maintain an armed body of constabulary tocoerce a majority, and expect it to behave like a police force whose duty is to protect the ninety- nine respectable persOns against one criminal. You cannot reduce your magistrates to the level of removable officials and yet preserve the same in- tegrity which is the honour of an independent magistracy. All our own institutions assume contented and a loyal people, in harmony with Government which it can chang.a at will. These institutions will not work in the atmosphere of
Irish misery.

It ties a concrete instance to show how far our institutions can degenerate under a system of perpetual coercion. The story of Sergeant SFLravAN hardly reads like a chapter of British history. It was not an isolated case. Sergeant SHERIDAN, who obtained the conviction of four innocent men by perjury, escaped scot•free, and was not even prosecuted. He had four police accomplices. Some of them are stilt in the force, and those who resigned received "compassionate allowances "—in ptain words, hvish money. trast their rate with that of Constable Con- trast London policeman who was sentencod to five years penal servitude the other day for a comparatively mild and wholly unsuccessful crime of the same type. The moral is clear. You cannot afford to maintain the same standard of justice in Ireland and in the United Kingdom. It is to these per- jured agents that we entrust the administration of coercion. They msy stop a public meeting by raising their right hands, and their testimony will suffice to send a Member of Parliament to hard labour. It is a perpetual system of martial law, a war of conquest that is never ended. ' SEVENTEEN years ago Lord SALISBURY told LIS that all Ireland required was twenty years Of reso- lute government. That piscription has been followed. And what is the result ? Is Ireland happier, richer, more contented ? Have we been able to relax our grip or govern Dublin a little more nearly as Edinburgh is governed? Our methods are more arbitrary than ever. Has Irish opinion been converted? On the contrary, the Irish party is again as united as it was under

PARNELL, and it attracts to its ranks not a few members who are educated and well connected. I It is among the Irish Unionists that the defection has begun. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, who did more to I defeat Home Rule than any living man save Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, is HOW the ally of MT. REDMOND, and behind him stand all the tenant-farmers of Ulster. He is not yet exactly a Home Ruler, but even he advocates a distinct Irish Parliament— which, however, he wishes to see at Westminster instead of Dublin. He tells us frankly that helhas learnt to respect the Irish members whom he used to distrust,and to detest the Irish landlords whom he followed in 1885. There are the fruits of resolute government. Will three years more make any difference? But that is not all. Even the least sympathetic Unionist has come to see that the Imperial Parliament, which has to watch over the affairs of en Empire vaster by many millions of subjects that it was in 1885,is not the '1 proper tribunal to govern Ireland. It lacks the time, the knowledge, and the sympathy. It might as well try to legislate for Newfoundland or Tasmania. And in attempting an impossible task it wrongs not only Ireland but itself. Out of the first eight days of a session which was to have been devoted to an English Education Bill it has had to give the greater part of four to Ireland— not of its own free will,but because eighty resolute and clever men can drive a wedge into even the stolidest wall of prejudice and indifference. Until we make up our minds to deal finally with the Irish land question by buying out the land lords,to remove the grievances of a judicial and police system worthier of Russia than of Britain, and to grant the Irish the same self-government which we have promised to the Boers, the deadlock and the friction, the misery and the disloyalty, are bound to continue.

WHAT is the amount of An • Inadequate gratitude that ought to Concession. be expressed for a con- cession which concedes Gnly the minimum of a just demand? The question arose in the House of Commons in connection with an amendment moved by Mr HENRY HOBHOUSE and accepted by the Government. The member for East Somerset who is one of the supporters of the administra- tion, proposed that assistant teachers and pupil teachers may, "if it is thought fir," be appointed to schools not provided by the local authority without reference to:their:creed or denomination.Mr BALFOUR agreed, and we may suppose that a glow of conscious virtue and highinindedness suffused itself over the Ministerial benches. " H ere," Conservative members must have said to them- selves, "Is a real boon for those troublesome Non- conformists. It is actually made possible for managers of Church of England schools to appoint them to inferior positions as teachers. What more do they want? What more would it be possible for us to offer them ? " Certainly the amendment is a real improvement on the Educa- tion Bill as it was originally framed, and it MI immediately accepted on that ground. The old adage about half a loaf beiag better than no bread has a peculiar application to important matters that are now being discussed at Westminister • The opponents of the Bill take what they can get for the moment, with a reasonably sure and certain hope that they will get something more later on. But as was said by Mr S. T. EVANS who has hardly been less distinguished in op- position to this Bill than Mr. LLOYD GEORGE, the authors of these feeble and partial, and to a large extent illusive concessions, must not expect too much in the way of gratitude. For example, they must not expect the opponents of the Bill— meaning the whole of the occupants of the Liberal benches—to approach them with bonded knees and whispering hunibleness, with the purpose of thanking them for a possible but problematical admission of Nonconformist teachers to second and third and fourth rate positions in Church of England schools, whilst excluding non-members of the Church of England from the post of head-master or head-mistress throughout two- thirds of the scliools of the country. Conces- sions of this kind are hypocritical. There is behind them the probably very sound convic- tion that a majority of deneca inational managers will take very precise care teat the " may "in Mr HOBHOUSE'S amendment shall be read as "must not." They are also, as Mr Wilt TLEY maintained, an insult to individual; convictions. "Every Nonconformist is branded as a person who can rise so far and no further in the calling that he has chosen to follow." They are, in addition, an obvious and glaring national wrong. The 'understanding on which they are based closes the teaching profession to many of the most fit, for who will choose a profession in which he can never hope to rise above the second place? "How many Nonconformists are going to become teachers," Mr CHARLES TREVELYAN, asked " when they know that all the highest places are closed to them ?" How many indeed ? And yet the Government and Mr Hosnousc were pained because the boon was accepted without effusive expressions of gratitude. There was indignation even when Mr. SAM EVANS proposed that the " may " in Mr. Hoenousn's amendment should gibe place to " shall." This was quite moderate remodelling of the proposition acquired by Sir WILLIAM ANSON for the Government. It secured nothing for non-Churchmen beyond a possibility of appointment as lower grade teachers in denomi- national schools. There still remained the quali- fying phrase," if it is thought fit." The school managers had everything left in their hands, as formerly. They were simply not obliged to appoint a Churchman as assistant master or as pupil teacher if they considered some applicant who was not a Churchman to be more deserving of the position. However, Mr. BALFOUR per- ceived in Mr. EVANS'S proposal something which would absolutely destroy the denominational character of the schools, and as he has previously informed us, the: preservation of: the denom- inational character of the r, chools is " the very root and principle "of the Education Bill. It is,of course, hopeless to endeavour to buy off the oppo- sition to the measure by such meagre delusive concessions as that of Mr. HOBHOU3E. It is to "the very root and principle of the" Bill that ob- jection is made. The Opposition in the House of COnarnOns is fighting against the re-imposition of a series of religious tests, and at the same time it is fighting for an effective as against an inferior and denominational system of education. The question of the appointment of teachers is the one really vital question still left as a subject for con- tention. It is what the Ulster loyalists who pro- posed to kick the Queen's Crown into the sea ' described as " the last ditch." It is a noble and will become a memorable battleground. Cardinal
