div.head: EXAMINER FRIDA y OCTOBER 31. 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDA y OCTOBER 31. 1902
VAVGHAN speaks of "the Government triumph over the Nonconformists." He is too previous. The victory is as yet far from being complete.

The Warrington Town Council as at present constituted met for the last time on Tuesday even- ing, when there were the usual ingenuous election speeches, from several memSrs who have to go to the poll to-day, and the vote of thanks to the Mayor for his services during the past twelve months. Alderman Sutton, on whom the mantle of the "father of the Council "—ex-Alderman Harrison—has fallen, was deputed to move the valedictory resolutic.a, and in suitable terms he expressed the indebtedness of the Council and the town to His Worship for the services he has rendered with so much care an assiduity during the year. The Deputy-Mayor seconded and eulogised the work of his successor to the office of chief magistrate, at the same time paying a courteous tribute to the Mayoresses of recent years. There is no doubt that the town owes Mr Parr much gratitude for his services. Few men, afilicted with bodily infirmity as he is, would have put their own desires so much on one side in order to serve the community. Mr Parr's record of attendances alone is an eloquent testimony to the extent of his labours. We hope he will have the same cordial support and encouragement during his second year as he has had in the period just brought to a close.

Tramway matters loom large nowadays in the business with which the Council, at its monthly meetings, has to deal. The Tramways Commit- tee on Tuesday submitted the report of Colonel von Donop, C.E., on his recent inspection of the Wilderspool route. Satisfaction is expressed with the system and the arrangements for safeguarding the public at the crossing,while a maximum speed of ten miles an hour is, we notice, imposed on that portion of the line where the cars usually travel at about 17 miles per hour. Speed regu- lations are excellent things and do much to render ttamways thoroughly efficient—when they are not adhered to !

The Chairman of the Committee (Alderman Roberts) replied to some inquiries by Councillor Tinnion in regard to the extension to Victoria- square, Stockton Heath, and from the Alderman's remarks the ratepayers will note, doubtless with gratification, that under the new arrangement the estimated cost of the scheme has been reduced from £ll,OOO to £7,000. This is a considerable reduction, but the sum is still an excessive one, considering the short length of the extension. However, the difficulties which beset the task ' account for the expense involved. The extension is a very necessary one, and will not only con- venience the large suburban populace of Stockton Heath, but it is sure to increase considerably the revenue from the cars. Alderman Roberts also defended the Sunday trams, and gave the reasons which induced the Committee to come to a deci- sion which, he believes, is absolutely right.

Mr. R. A. Naylor has sent us a large-sized 45- page pamphlet entitled Summary of Complaint re Thelwall Nuisance." It is an imposing prcduc- tion and the amount of evidence it iontains on this vexed and vexing question is stupendous. One cannot for a moment imagine that the Local Government Board has not already been to some extent impressed with the voluminousness of the complaints and the gravity of the charges against this notorious nuisance, but the Board gives little encouragement to the sufferers. Possibly Mr. Naylot's new publication, with its damning mass of evidence and trenchant opinion, may succeed where smaller efforts have feed. It is difficult to believe that a self-respecting authority could ( ignore the appeal from these pages, and even if the Local Government Board remains adamant surely I the Runcorn Rural Councillors will be affected when they received their copies of this interesting " summary." If it induces nothing else it is likely to affl;ct the guilty councillors with a nightmare which may bring about repentance, and, happily erformance.

Igame. They contented themselves with purely de- fensive tactics and attacked with vigour but a few isles during the match. There were unfortunately t great many penalty kicks which spoiled what might have been an open game. The real truth is that Cheshire were overplayed at every point. On the winning side, Fish played superbly, his dan gerous runs baffling all but the stone wall Houghton Wilson too played a plucky game, wkile Valentine by no means got along as well as he might have done. With but one or two mistakes Smith played soundly. The br3thers James showed all their old dash and trickiness, out-manoeuvring entirely Booth ond Richardson. The former player was but an indifferent substitute for Jolley, while Richardson hardly played up to his usual style. Jones was perhaps the best man of the losing team, Houghton as usual playing a grand game.

LBY A CORRESPONDENT'.

The newly inaugurated branch of the Y M C A.at Earlestown seems to be going swimmingly. It was certainly sent off with a great Hare of trumpets,and if it only continues as it commenced, it should be one of the most successful branches in the neigh- bourhood. The Yen Archdeacon Madden, at the public meeting which was held in the Town Hall; gave some excellent advice seasoned with poignant home thrusts, It was all very well, he said, to applaud the remarks which were made by the speakers, but would they, he asked, pay their sub- I scriptions. This was going straight home, and according to all accounts, the observation was not relished. He was, however, not far off the mark. A good many of those at the meeting had not the remotest idea of joining the association, but were simply present to listen to the Yen Archdeacon.

I should think the promoters of the Cottage Hospital Bazaar feel pretty well disgusted with the result as disclosed by the balance sheet. It is in- conceivable that to gain £l4O the expenses should total up to nearly twice the amount. There must have been some reckless expenditure somewhere, and I consider the public have a right to know how it has come about. So far they have not been taken into the confidence of the promoters, which augurs badly for the success of any future undertaking of the kind.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

After a week's rest Earlestown took the field oil Saturday at home against Southport Central. This is the second occasion this season on which they have encountered the sand grounders, and,as on the first meeting, they were defeated. As showing the relative strength of the teams, Southport won on their own ground by 3 goals to nil, whilst on Saturday as visitors they won by 3 goals to 1, It was said the first defeat was due to the composi- Lion of the Earlestown term, which was not con- sidered to be so strong as usual, but this can hardly be accepted as an excuse, when on Saturday the strongest team they could put in the field was beaten by nearly the same number of points. A new player, Brown, from St Helens Town, was tried at centre forward, and he proved a remark- ably bard worker. He is fairly fast,and he kept the wings well up, but he lacks judgment somewhat. For instance on Saturday, he had possession of the ball, and was in an easy position for scoring, with practically an open goal, but for some unaccount- able reason he made no attempt to score, but slung the ball over Co the wing and of course ruiued what appeared to be a splendid chance. Settle played a capital game throughout,but he was not sufficiently supported b 3 Leigh. Jones at full back was not by any means a Success, and the sooner Limond gets into harness again the better it will be for the club They have some stiff encounters before them yet, and will need to play a more combined game if they intend to secure any measure of success.

Newton were also at home on Saturday with Birkenhead, and judging from the result of the game, were a little to good for the seaport town. It is a pity however.these combina- tion teams cannot get through their matches with- out so much squabbling. It may perhaps, to some extent, be the :fault of the referee, and this is a point the Combination Committee might well look to.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

P.S.A. The weekly meeting of the Earlestown and dis- trict P.S.A., was held on Sunday at the Co-opera- tive Hall. There was a good attendance, Dr Latham presiding. Mr Gilling of Ashton was the principal speaker and gave an intereating address. Vocal selections were given by Mr Charles Hatton, and recitations by Mr Williams. Miss Williamson pre- sided at the piano.

div.head: LIVERPOOL FARM SCHOOL.
div.p: LIVERPOOL FARM SCHOOL.

On Tuesday evening the lads of the Liverpool Farm School, Newton-le-Willows were entertained by the choir of the Manchester City Mission at Earlestown. Mr Dring, the missioner, conducted the entertainment, the subject of his lecture being the " Life of Charles Garrett" the Wesleyan Metho- dist Evangelistic preacher. Mr A Dring the choir- master acted as accompanist. After the lecture Miss Smith recited "The dying boy " and "The water mill." Mr Digweed returned thanks for the attendance of the choir. ST PETER'S CHURCH —PAROCHIAL TEA AND CONCERT.

The annual parochial tea aud concert in con- nection with St Peter's, Newton, took place on Thursday evening. About 150 sat down to tut which was served in the schoolroom, the lady mem- bers of the congregation presiding at the tables, After tea a move was made to the Town Hall, where an excellent programme was submitted. Miss Bodmer and Mr E Leyland opened with a pianoforte duet" Grand March.' Mr S Dring followed with an excellent rendering of " The Windmill." A 'cello solo " Simple Avon " by Miss Airey was nicely given. Miss Corlett afterwards sang " Abide with me." A recitation in the Lancashire dialect, en- titled " Baur Folks" by Mr J H Lane caused much amusement, as also did 'Cuddle Doon " which he recited as an encore. Miss Bodmer rendered "Awake " in good style; and Mr D Thorp was deservedly applauded for a well performed violin solo. The humorous song by Mr S Smith " Maud, Maud, Maud," (from Iforeador ")brought the first part of the programme to a close. After a short interval Miss Bodmer gave a pianoforte solo, Mr Welsh following with a ;song entitled " Anchored." Miss Corlett and Mr S Dring gave a duet in fine style and an instrumental trio " Spring song" by Miss Airey and Messrs Thorp and Leyland was nicely rendered. A recita- tion" The new church organ" by Mr J H Lane was ! well received. Miss Corlett sang "Good-bye," and Mr S Dring 'The Bandolero." Mr S Smith also contributed another humorous song. The singing of the National Anthem brought the concert to a close. nAILLESTOWN, NEWTON, HAYDOCIT, &c , BUILDING

div.head: SOCIETY.
div.p: SOCIETY.

The 39th annual meeting of this society was held in the District schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr Thomas Haselden, president of the committee, presided, and there was a fair attendance of mem- bers. The report and balance sheet showed that the profit for the year amounted to £1,955 17s lid, which with the undivided balance from last year of £2,802 13s 2d,leit a disposable profit of £4758 Its ld, out of which the Directors recommended the pay- ment of a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent per annum absorbing £1,838 15s Sc! and leaving a balance of undivided profit of £2,919 15s Bd, being ,an increase over last year of £ll7 2s 63. Three members had redeemed their property, represent- ing repayments of capital amounting to £1,556 53.. There was one lot of propertk on hand, consisting of 18 houses, situate at Thatto Heath. The number of members on the books was 413, holding 4,0521 shares.— ' The Chairman said thevlwould'see they had realised a profit of almost £2,ooo,from which their directors proposed to pay a dividend of 5 per cent on all paid up shares. This would leave a balance of about £1,700 which they proposed to add to the reserve fund, making this fund close upon £3,000 wlicti he considered was decidedly satisfactory.He moved the adoption of the report and statement of accounts.— Mr Monks seconded and the motion was adopted.— The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr i Thomas Haselden was re-elected Chairman of the committee, and .the following were appointed directors, Messrs W Gilmour. John Barr, John Walker, Henry Sweetlove, W H Bailey, B Harrison, J Cook, D Barcroft, T Orman& Mr Eli Bunting was re-appointed surveyor; Messrs T Thomp•on and W Appleby, auditors. Messrs H Tarbuck and J Goad- ing were appointed stewards. VIADUCT INRTITUTII, EARLESTOWN. _

On Thursday evening the. periodical concert in connection with the above was held in the Insti- tute. As is usually the case at these concerts, the room was packed to its utmost capacity long before the concert commenced. , Mr J A Partington officia- ted at the piano, and opened the proceedings by an overture, entitled " Gems from the Opera.' In his rendering of " Mona" which followed, Mr Giovanni Raffo displayed a splendid tenor voice. Miss Marion Lee was precluded from Attending. and her place was filled by Madame Aston A humorous sketch, entitled " Society and Variety," by Mr Harry Lawton, proved par- ticularly palatable to the audience, as 8190 did the wonderful exhibition of whistling by Mr Derby- shire Wincklev, the latter artiste rendering a solo entitled " Gage d'Amour," whilst, as an inevitable encore, he gave imitations of various song birds. Miss Kate Trevor afterwards sang "There's a land," which was followed by a clever exhibition of shad- ography by Mr J L Wyman. A humorous sketch by Mr Harry Lawton, entitled "Musical Bob," brought the programme to a close. The Institute Committee are to be complimented on getting up such an en- joyable entertainment, all tastes being capitally catered for. The humorist proved to be one of the best seen in Earlestown for some time, whilst both 'the whistler and conjurer were extremely clever. THE MAKERFIELD AMATEUR DEAMA.TIC SOCIETY.

The second venture of the above Society in the direction of amateur theatricals, in the form of Still Wafers Run Deep" and "Cricket on the Hearth," which have been staged at the Town Hall, Earlestown, during this week, has not up to the present received he support it deserves. On Mon- day night, the occasion n. the production of " Still Waters Run Deep," the Hall was scarcely half filled, whilst the following night, when the " Cricket on the Hearth " occupied the boards, the attendance was every whit as poor, if not worse. Such a state of things must, of course, prove intensely disap- pointing to the artistes, and considering that the proceeds are to be devoted to local charities, the Management have every right to expect better sup- I port. It is to be hoped that to-night (Friday) and to-morrow night, will see the Hall better filled than it has been on any of the previous nights. Both plays are extremely well-staged, several of the artistes displaying unmistakable talent, although the elocution is not quite what it might be. " Still Waters Run Deep "—described as a comedy in three acts, commenced the week's , run on Monday night, and the piece was very capably handled by the amateurs. On Tuesday night a farce entitled " The Tourist Ticket" opened the proceedings, the many laugh- able scenes in this proving extremely palatable to the audience, The " Cricket on the Hearth " was very powerfully produced,the performance being a highly succeqsful one, and well worth going to see. _ The Chairman of the Petty Sessions on Monday (Mr E J Norman) said,that befoTe commencing the ordinary business of the Court he had a pleasing duty to perform. This was to present a framed certificate of the Royal Liverpool Soipwreck and Humane Society, to Elwin Harrison,aged 19 years, of English-row. It happened that on the Ist June two little girls fell into the Bridgewater Canal and Harrison at the risk ot his life rescued them. lie and his fellow magistrate,Mr Taylor,were pleased to present the certificate and in common with all their fellow townsmen were proud that they had so brave a man amongst them.—llarrison who is full back to the Runcorn "A" team thanked their worships.

PUBLIC BRNBFIT UNDIIR TOLOOK FOR MIST BOOTS IN LANCA SHlRll.—Advt INFRINGING THE SWINE FEVER ACT. At the Runcorn Petty Sessiors on Monday Catherine Grine, an old woman, was charged with having caused a sow to be moved without the necessary declaration.—William Parker a youth was charged with moving the sow.—P C Upton said that on the 21st October Parker came with the sow in his cart with a note from Mrs Grice asking him to make out the necessary licence. The licence should have been obtained first and the sow should not have been taken to his (Upton's) house without the necessary permit. There was no attempt to evade the law.—The defendant said she did not intend to commit an offence, and was sorry she had unwittingly erred.—The case against the boy was dismissed and Mrs Grice was fined 10s includ- ing costs.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

It is interesting to record the fact that owing to absence of members the Brunswick Mutual Improve- ment Class did not hold their weekly meeting on Wednesday week it being the first time in the forty years history of the society that this has .occurred,

Educational matters are proceeding apace in Runcorn. The local voluntaryists have now taken to the war path so that there is every anticipation that before long there will be a collision some- where, somehow. It was of course, a great occa- sion for the clerical party the other day when the bishop of the Diocese visited the town. Nerved by his august presence some of the local speakers plucked up courage not only to defend their own side,but to actually carry the war into the enemy's camp. On the whole the speAches were of but an indifferent quality and do not in any sense do justice to their authors, who are all capable of pro- ducing something better.

All the speakers in gcneral and one in particular revelled in the extreme measures of justice which will be brought to bear on those who for " con- science sake" refuse to pay the new educational rate. What a blessing it is that the clericals have at last got hold of something which affords them satisfaction. Just as small things amuse small minds so the harsh ecclesiastical character glories in cruel and tyrannical extremes,misnamed justice.

I believe that the London Executive Council have sent down to the Runcorn Free Church Council forms for the enrollment of those who will refuse to pay the new Church rate. It will be interesting to know the decision of the local Council on the matter,and it is to be hoped that the secretary, Mr Millington, will convene the Council at the earliest possible moment to consider the matter. For the honour of Nonconformist Runcorn, let the Free Church Coulon act promptly and firmly in this momentous issue.

Halton Court Leet is one of those hardy annuals which are always welcome as a remembrancer of ancipnt days. Though the glory of the old Court has very largely departed, its quaint ceremony will never fail to be of interest to tne outsider an less than to the antiquarian. The ancient court was opened on Saturday with but a shadow of its former splendour but it "'still com- manded the attention of many of the hamlets which once fell under its sway so that there was an extremely representative attendance. May the old court long continue to re-associate us with that past which is linked an firmly with the present.
FOOTEALL.

The match on Saturday between Lancashire and Cheshire could by no means be termed a great game. All the elements were present that might have constituted a record exhibition but instead of chere being a unification among the elements there was decidedly the reverse. The earlier stages of the , game really saw Cheshire more tban holding their own and their opponents showing an utter lack of cohesion. It was, however, but for a moment, figuaratively speaking, that this disorganization prevailed, and once the reds got into the awing of the game Cheshire cut a very sorry figure indeed. A set of forwards were never more hopelessly beaten than those represent- ing the Cheese County. Five times out of every six the visiting contingent gathered the leather and but for a very keen defence there would have been a much heavier defeat to bewail. Somehow or other it appeared as though the Cheshire team from the first were not trying to play a winning

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
Good Templars and Councillor Ellison's Action in Latchford.

At the weekly meeting of the Temperance Migsion Lodge of the 1.0.G.T. held in Ebenezer Church on Wed- nesday, the following resolution was pissed after a long and earnest discussion :—That this meeting of the Tem- perance Mission Lodge of the Independent Order of Good Template greatly reg6t the step taken by Coun- cillor Luke Ellison with retard to the candidature of Mr W B Roberts in Latchford Ward and do not countenance his action in any way."—At the weekly session of the Latchford Lodge of the LO.G.T. the following resolution was unanimously adopted :—"That this meeting of Good Templars Arenuously oppose the return of Mr W B Roberts to the Town Council, as the election of the gentleman would not be conducive to the advancemeat of temperance principles in the town. div.head: Mr. Docids Replies to Councillor
div.p: Mr. Docids Replies to Councillor
Tinnion.

Evidence of the interest which is being taken in to-day's contests was afforded by the crowed atten- dance at a meeting of the electors of the Town Bewsey and Orford Wards. favourable to the stoppage of all trading by members of the Council direct or indirect, with the Corporation, which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-street, on Tuesday evening. Mr B Bindloss presided and there were present on tuel platform the Rev E T Reed, and Messrs Norbury Williams,James Dodds (candidate for the Town Hall Ward). S Gough (candidate for Bewz-ey Ward), J Pemberton (candidate for Latchford Ward), Alfred Ilulme, and Joseph ft Turner (St. Helens). THE CHAIRMAN AND TFIE TOWN COUNCILLORS' OBJECT.
THE ACTION OF TtIE LIBERALS IN LATCHFORD WARD.

In the course of his address the CHAIRMAN ;aid he took that crowded meeting, which he trusted would be very enthusiastic, as an augury of their intention not only to place Mr Dodds and his friends at the head of the poll, but also to place them there with such an overwhelming majority as would show to their masters and dictators at the Town Hall that they had Chown off once and for all the shackles of political slavery and once more stood forth as free men. They had been singing their song for the past twelve months and the time for action bad now arrived. They would agree with him that when they saw a great meeting like that one they could not imagine for one single moment, in fact it would be a disgrace to their feelings to so imag- ine, the possithlity of not returning their friends at the rhead of the poll. But all our troubles of past history and the present troutle of the war in Somaliland arose from our aptness to under-estimate our enemies. They could easily imagine 50 or 100 voters saying that Mr Dodds was so sure of his return that there was no neces- sity for them to vote. It was that sort of thing, how- ever,that brought ruin to the best causes,and he begged and implored that every one of them would turn up and do their duty like freeborn Englishmen on the day of the poll. (Applause). Could they have a better champion in the whole of Lancashire, or indeed in the whole of England, than Mr James Dodds ?—(" No" and applause.)-1 man whose hand was always open to the cry of the poor and needy, a min of unostentatious charity, who had always been the foe of everything that was shady and wrong, and mean and treacherous, who had fought their lbattles through thick and thin at groat cost to himself of time and trouble. (Applause.) Above all, he would be the right man in the right place at the present moment because be was a trained accountant, and he thought n 3 man could be better at figures in the whole of England. Therefore he was the man of all others whom they should pet in at a time like the present. He (the speaker) had not lived in Warrington very long, but:it appeared to him that it had been the object and ambition of every man elected to the Warrington Town Councl to spend as much of the ratepayers' bard-earned taxes as was possible in bricks and mortar' and slates and tiles. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said that campaign had been fought in a gentlemanly way, and nothing had been said about the private life, history, or actions of any man. When a man entertsi into public life. however, his actions became public property, and what he did, they (his hearers) and everybody else bad a perfect right to criti- cise and pass their opinions upon. He was convinced that he had never heard in hie life of a more despicable and shameless thing than the present state of affairs in the Latchford Warn. Here was an illustration of what they had been trying to combat during the last n months. Their good friend Mr Pemberton, who had fought and hung on with the pertinacity of a British bulldog, was put forward as a Conservative candidate for the Latchford Ward. Then another party—a brewer and, he believed, a Cooservative—was brought forward by some means or other as an Independent candidate. He (the speaker) was not a teetotaller, nor had he got a word to say against any brewer in the world. This gentleman was however, supported by the Liberal branch and the teetotallers of the Latchford Ward. (Laughter). He believed they called themselves a branch of the great Liberal Party, but if they were a branch they must be a mighty rotten and mean branch. (Applause). He had always had an idea—rightly or wrongly—that the Liberals had always stood in the front holding up the banner of truth, uprightness,peace and justice, and he would not be surprised to know that some gentleman who was connected with this sort of thing was at that moment among the audience at the Parr Hall, or perhaps on the platform, preaching and advocating the cause of peace, justice, uorightness and honour, and seeking that the Education Bill should be sent to the mischief. (Laughter.) Did they think Chet state of things was proper ? Had these Latchford Liberals any conscience? It seemed to him that they were being led like "lambs to the slaughter-house or were going voluntarily to the slaughter-house and cutting their own throats. Such things as these, however, came back to roost sooner or later, and they might depend upon it that not very much later these Latchford so-called Liberals and tee- totallers would find out their mistake and meanwhile they stood exposed to the mockery and derision of every free man in England. In c soclasion the chairman urged upon his hearers the 'overt which they possessed as electors.
MR. DODDS REPLIES TO COUNCILLOR TINNION. NOT A SINGLE WORD OF TRUTH IN THE STATEMENT ABOUT BEWSEY WARD.

Mr DODDS delivered a very brief address. He said he must refer to a statement made by Councillor Tinnion at a meeting held in St Austin's Ward the previous night. That gentleman seemed to have got into hot water all round lately from the reckless way in which he had been misrepresenting several people. He was reported at a meeting on Monday evening to have said that he (Mr Doddi) proposed or suggested that Mr Brophy I should allow his name to sttn I before the constitu-ncy until a minute or two before the time of withdrawal and then withdraw hie name, and Mr Thornton would be left, and he would naturally ge in to represent Bewsey Ward. Need he say that there was not a word of truth in the statement? Nor was there a word of truth in the statement that he sought Councillor Tinnion on the telephone, or in any other way, in regard to the matter. The simple explanation was that on September 30th last he received a letter from the leading Liberal in the borough asking him if he would help Councillor Tinnion and CouncTor James Evans in regard to their re-election on the lit November. Following this letter Councillor Tinnion called on him four times with thd sele object of inducing him to induce the Non-Trading Committee not to oppose his return. Al though not unfavourable, he could not undertake to go against his committee. He was loyal to it, and this attack on him was the result-. He assured them he knew nothing whatever stout den- tioneeriug dodges, he knew nothing as to scheming nom- inationa and withdrawals—Councilkr Tinnion did not speak from his own knowledge. Councillor Tinnion was not present when he (the speaker) was supposed Co have made the statement he attributed to bim,acd yet he had no hesitation in launching a charge against him which was absolutely and entirely false. (Applause.) He was not going into the qoestion as to whether he was in a false pesition in regard to his candidature for the Town Hall Ward. He had no shares in any firm that had ever traded with the Corporation, nor did the position he held depend upon the business his company did ; hence he was absolutely safe in regard to either im- tr oral or illegal trading. But apart from the strict legality and morality f his positron, th.re was not a man in Warrington who did net know in his heart that if there should ever be any donbt at all as to the abso- lute propriety of his position, he would not remain longer in it. (Applause.) He had not sought the candidature, he was not canvassing a single elector,and he assured them he should never do anything to forfeit the confidence which his fellow townsmen had reposed in him. (Applause.) MR. A. HULME AND MR. S. GOUGH.

The nexC speaker was Mr A HULME who criticised the remarks of CauocillcrA Evans and W Roberta uttered the previous evening. Referring to Mr Upson,Mr Rulnae said he was sound on " no-trading " and would be a valuable acquisition to the Council. Mr G Ale) had stood before for Bewsey Ward and he had never had a fraction of the votes he ought to have bad.

div.head: DENIALS BY MR. PEMBERTON.
div.p: DENIALS BY MR. PEMBERTON.

Mr PEMBERT:N said be wished to answer some charges which had been made against him m rLain paper It charged him with doing contracts for a putlic body with which be WM connected-That was a grass untruth. He had ozly one contract, and he was riot a member of the body which hal given it ote. Be bad never been within miles of it. he did not sit on its Boara, he had no connection with it whatever,and be had no tuend there. L: was that body that summoned him to D rosbury, so he did not think they were very favourable to him. He was also charged with opposing Mr CW Davenport, te Conservalive caudiaate ior the District Council. That was another untruth. That contest was never fought on pa;itical grounds. All the literature was printed in black ink aLct politics were never mentioned on either side. Another charge was that be opposed a Conserva— tive for County Ciuncil honours. That s, as untrue,for the reason that he never fought at all. He was never even ncminated. Be only made these explanations so that everyone should kaow the true positim ot affairs. (Applause ) SPEECH BY MR TURNER OF ST HELENS.

Mr TURNER addressed the meeting, and said he had come there to support Mr Dodds, not because of any particular political views he might bold, but because he (the speaker) had al along been strongly of tte opinion that politics should nave nothing to do with municipal affairs. (Applause). He urgen his hearers to &elect as members of the Council men of the right type with large limas, who took a sympathetic interest in everything that coucein-A the weitaie of the town,men with true business instincts and with education. (Applause.)

Illicit Lead-Buying Warrington Men Fined At Widnes, on Thursday, Alfred FJzzard, marine store dealer, Frederick -street, was charged with baying a quantity of lead from tW) Widnes publicans,en the 25th September, which was under 1 cwt. The offence was admitted, but defendant pleaded ignorance of the law, as he had only been in the business for six weeks. A fine of 55 an costs was imposed. William Plinston and Henry Chorley zuarine-store dealers, of Warrington, were charged with buying 66ibs of lead from Fozzard, the quantity being under weight. Plinston was fined 403 and costs, or, in default, fourteen days. Chorley was mulcted in the sum of 5s and ccats. Warrington Technical Institute. The prizes offered by the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes,on the result of the examiaa- tions held in the spring has just been distribizteds The list includes the names of two Warrington students, Miss Julia E Weber, who obtained the first prize for German (elementary stage), and Miss Ina Carr who receives the third prize (divided) for French (elementary stage.)

Another Tail-Light Prosecution. George 'Whatley, 43, Eldon-street, Warrington was summoned at Dareshury Sessions on Tuesday for failing to carry a lighted lamp showing a red light attached to the rear of a lurry of which he was in charge on September 24th—Mr Browne pleaded" not guilty " on behalf of the defendant. —P C Williams stated that he saw the defendant in charge of a horse and two lames at 9.25 pm. at Grappenhall. There was no red light attached to the back of the last lurry. The length of the waggon was as near as possible twelve feet. On the back hairy there was a float,on which were two lights, and one of these was afterwards pat on the back of the lurry.—By Mr llrowne : The first lurry was loaded, and the second was merely a show lorry. He contended that the lorry projected 12 feet behind the other lurry,and there:was no lamo on it. For the defence. Mr Browne said he admitted all the ' facts. Mr Muskett was returning from Altrincham Snow on the date in question and engaged the de- fendant's employers to take the lorries back to Walton. The first one contained sign boards, au the second was merely a show l lorry, and therefore he contended that these was no projection behind. Mr Muskett had no intention ot evading the bylaw whatever.—The Chairman said the Bench had de- cided that there WAS no intention to break the by- law, but that there was a projection, atol the de- fendant would be fined in the costs.

Warrington Liberal Club. There was a very satisfactory report to submit at the annual meetiag ef the Warrington Liberal Club held on Monday evening. Mr A H Crosileld (the President) was unable to be present, and the Chair- man of the Club Committee (Councillor Tinnion) was enoged in addressing the ele2tors of St. Austin's Ward. In the circumstances the chair was taken by Mr J Worrell The Secretary (Mr Thomas Pemberton) read the list of attendances of the Committee during the past year, and said the Club had lost two valuable members by the death of Mr John Crostleld and Air Councillor Plumpton. He was pleased to be able to report that the past year had been a record one in all departments, except in the bowliag, the cause being the short and wet season and the large expense on improve- ments. The Committee hoped that next year the green would be second to none The balance sheet of the Club showed a substantial balance la hand. (Applause) She Secretary's report and balance sheet were adopted on the motion of Mr W Jeffrey, seconded ty Conncillor Wilkinson, and supported by the Chairman.—Ths folio wing officers were re-elected :—President and treasurer, Mr A. II Cros- field ; vice-presidents, Councillors Tinnion, Pier- point, and Wilkinson ; hon. secre'arv, Mr Thomas Pemberton; committee, Messrs J Beaman. George Beard, W Bibby, J Chappell, J Davies, G fl Slum, Georze Strange, E V Walker, and J Worrell ; audi- tov, Messrs John Harrison and W Ford.

div.head: THAMwAYS. -- 1 he Wilderspool Route.
div.p: THE THAMwAYS. -- 1 he Wilderspool Route.
Board of Trade Inspector's Report. Stockton Heath Extension.

At the meeting of the Town Council, on Tuesday evening, the Tramways Committee submitted the report of Lieuten sat Colonel von Donop, R. 8., on his inspec- tion ot the Wilderspool section of the Corporation Tram- ways, together with the Board of Trade'a certificate that to tramways are fit for the purlic traffic. Colonel von Donop's report states that "the lines are constructed paecisely similar to those previously inspected at Warrington, and the same ears are to te used on them. Tramway No. 10 crosses the L. Sz. N. W. Railway line on the • level,and special safety precautions have been provided to guard against accidents at this crossing. At points of fifty yards on each side of the level crossing there are switches fixed, which are worked by the signal man in the railway signal box, anLi by means of which the signal man can cut off the current from that section en;irely. A semaphore signal is provided for each line of tramway, and there is the customary interlocking between these signals and the gates similar to that between the railway signals and the gates. One small alteration is requirsd ; it is arranged so that if a car comes to a stand after enter- ing the dead section it is then possible for the signalman to cut off the 'current, to put the tram signals to danger and to close the gates across the road; but if the electric lights in the car are alight it is not possible for him to do so; the London and North Western Railway asked that this might be altered so that the fact of the lamps being lighted should not take it out of the power of the signalman to cut oft the current, and the Corporation has agreed to make this alteration. In all other respects the arrangements seem quite satisfactory, and the Lon- don and North Western Railway are satisfied with them. Speed on these lines should be restricted to eight miles an hour, with the following exceptions : (1). Along the Wilderspool Road betwen the Black Lion Bridge and River-road, ten miles an hour. (2). Along the VVilderspool Mead when crossing the Brewery Level d NEMO., four miles an hour.

(3). Along the Wilderspool Read, between River- road and the Warrington Bridge, four miles an hear. ALDERAIAN ROBERTS ANC TrIE ARRANGEMENT want STOCKTON HEATH. At a recent meeting of the Tramways Committee, the Town Clerk reported that the differences with the Parish Council of Stockton Heath with regard to the Light Railway Order had been removed, and it was resolved that the Order be proceeded with, and that Messrs Preece and Cardew be instructed to peepers the necessary plans and estimates for the construction of Railway No 1 (from Stafford-road, )Vilderepool, to Victoria Square, Stockton Heath). Councillor Timms said it was reported some time ago that the Stockton Heath people wanted the Cor- peratios to do everything for them. He thought it was desirable that the Council should know what the terms were that had been agrees to,and what it was propesed to do. If they were going to proceed at once with the whole length between Stockton Heath and Latchford that was a matter he was not prepared to assent to. Alderman ROBERTS, the chairman of the Tramways Committee, said the explanation was very simple. The order which the Tramways Committee had taken up gave the assent of the Light Railway Commisseoners to two light railways—number one and number two. Number one was tee railway which connected up to the terminus of the Corporation tramway at Wilders- peel. and carried the work on to rthe Mulbsrry Tree at Stockton Heath. Number two, which they did net pro- pose to deal with at present, tormented from the Mulberry Tree to the swing bridge ac Latchford. In reference to the other matter, the proposals originally submitted by the Council had in effect been accepted by them. Under the conditions originally asked for by the Stockton Heath Parish Council number one railway would have cost £ll,OOO, but under the conditions now agreed to, the cost would be only £7,000. ALDERMAN ROBERTS AND SUNDAY CARS. At the meeting of the Warrioy,ton Town Council on Tuesday, Alderman Reberts, as chairman of the Tram- ways Committee, referred to the deehtion of the General Purposes Committee that they could not see their way to comply with the protests from the Methodist Free Church and the Warrington and District Christian Endeavour Union against the running of trams on Sunday. He remarked that he did not wish that the people representad by these protests should think that their proposals were treated with anythide other than respect. As the members of the Council were aware, the matter was very thoroughly discu ered in the General Purposes Committee and what he felt Was this that their good friends, whose opinions they all treated with every respect and whese sentiments they very largely agreed with in many regards, did not perhaps quite appreciate thedifficulty in which the town wouldbe plaited if their proposal were agreed to. In the first place they could not refuse to sanction the running of 'buses if there was no means of communication between differ- ent parts of the tewn and the suburbs such as were provided by the present trantwa3 serviso, and that being the case the object of the proposal of these good people if accepted would be entirely defeated. He him- self had noticed that while the trams certainly employed a certain meant of labour,it was considerably less than the labour employed by the 'buses, insomach as in the latter ease horses were used, and horses were just, as much entitled to rest as any other species of animal. (Hear, hear.) Then again a great many people used these trams for the purpose of attending places of wor- ship in the town, and they had also to remember that these services sif trains provided means of recreation for mealy whese opportanities for recreation during the week were extremely limited, and who did not make it a habit of attending a place of worship. It was far better that these men should get out into the country for an hour or two on Sunday than that they should stop in the town and spend their time in the public house. It was a delicate question, but he believed the I decision of the Tramways Committee to continue these Sunday serviees wee absolutely right. The resolution of the General Purposes Committee was approved by the Council.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS
Councill& Tinnion's Candidature,
Meeting in ,St Austin's Ward.
A Reply to The Non-Trading Committee.

Tne schoolroom in TOE!wlis-street was crowded on Monday evening on the occasion of a meeting in support of the candideturee of Mr Councillor Tinnier] and Mr Councillor James Evens for St Austin's and Whitecross Wards respectively. Councillor Barton presided and he was accemeanied on the platform by the two candidates mentioned and Councillor William Roberts and 'Messrs Nethen Cook William Crosskill and I El well, jai]. It may be stated that the meeting had been summoned before it was known that Mr Charles Longshaw had retired from the contest in Whitecross Ward reed allowed Councillor James Evans a we over. 1 Toe CHMRMAN referred to the erialifieetions Of Comm. oilier Tinnier' to represent St Austin's Ward. Even Mr , Dodds expressed himself as being willing to give Cons- ' milers Tinnier* and Evans a further lease of municipal life, but sneltered himself behiod somebody else, for he said that others who had, more experience of them than he (Mr D)dds) had had weigaed them in the balances and found them, as they thought, wanting Such evidence against men was worthless. It EIPMCOOd• to him (the chairman) that these friends of Mr Decide had weighed them in imaginary scales. (Laughter). Ha (the chairman) had had an opportunity of wechine the eonduct of Coun- cillors Tinninn and Evans on the Council and he was Iquite satisfied that they were the right men in the right place. They had discharged their duties in a way , which reflected great credit upon them and in a way that was satisfactory to the people who had returned them to the Council. (Hear, hear.) Teem were many politi- cal stars floating in the Warrington atmosphere at the present time. (Laughter.) He had seen political stars before,but never in his life had he seen a wannest' show so muddled awl mixed upas the political show which was on exhibition in Warrington just now. (eraughter.) He supposed some of these stars were only shootiug stars. (Laughter.) He believed they did so occasionally,but he was rather curious te know what these stars were going to shoot at. If they were going to shoot Councillors Tinnion and Evans out of the Town Council, he thoueht they would very muce miss their muk. They were just as likely to shoot the man out of .the moon. (Laugh- ter.) The Chairman proceeded to Wee to the important work transacted by the Town Council and stated that something like half a million of money passed through the hands of the Town Council every year. ThirtS-9fir members of the Council were responsible for that large sum which warked out at something like £13,000 per member. It was necessary to have level-headed men in the Council and he would advise them to stick to the old candidates of St Aultin's and Whitecrose Wards who had served them so well in the past and who would serve them well in the future. (Applause.) Councillor Tnerrroer, who had a hearty. reception, said he was there to give an account of his stewardship, and also to meet some of the calumnies and base neistepre- sentations which had been made in reference to himself and the Liberal party_ So far as his opponent was con- cerned he hoped they would be able to fight this battle and shake hands before they started, and shake hands after the pen was declared. (Pear, bear). He did not believe in throwing mud, because be thought it was a very peer way of fighting. (Hear, hear.) The Munici- pal Non-Trading Association had asked the Liberal party why they had not selected candidates in all the wards of the town. One reason why they had not selected them was because they could not get thein,and another reason was because they had asked everyone who was likely te be • candidate to pay his own expenses. He stood there bound to no association, bound to no individuals. He was prepared to fight for himself, to pay his own expenses and take the verdict of the ratepayers. (Applause). The Liberal party had been accused of not attempting to find candidates. They had tried tefind candidates for Latchford,Town Hall,Howley, Fairfield, and St John's Wards. Likely candidates were interviewed but none would become candidates for those Wards. He was there to say that so far as he was coecerned, there was no cempect between the two political parties at the present time. The Non-Trading Committee had also accused them of fighting those battles politically. He did not hesitate to say that municipal elections had been fought politically and on many occasions the best man had not been returned. He hoped the time was coming when • men would be returned, not because he was a Liberal or a Tory, but because he was the most intelligent and most fitting to represent the true interests of the ratepayers. (Applause.) Mr Dodds had chatged him with "wire- pulling in spite of his (Councillor Tinnion's) bare-faced deniale." That Was rather strong language for Mr Dodds to Use. He (Councillor Tinnion) had endeavoured to treat Mr Dodds with that respect which his position merited and he asked for the earns consideration from Mr Dodds. A few days ago Mr Dodd,' rang him up on the telephone and asked him why he was proposing a certain man for Bewsey ward. He (Councillor Tianion) replied that he had not proposed anyone and that the ward meeting had not been held. Mr Dodds intimated to him the the gentleman mentioned would not be acceptable to him (Mr Dodds). He (Councillor Tionion) saw Mr Dedds and told him that he would like him to be in the Town Councleand offered him a seat on behalf of the Liberal party in Howse? Ward.tdr Dodds declined, but suggested the name of Mr Henry Thornton as a candidate.Se(Councilor Tinnion)pronosed Mr Thornton anta candidate at the meeting of the Bewsey Ward Com- mittee,but the committee could not see its way to select him and finally adapted Mr John Brophy as the candi- date. Mr Decide sent for Mr John Brophy and made this suggestion to him. This was an instance of wire- pulling and wirepulling he (Courscillor Tionio a) would not be associated with. Mr Dodds proposed to Mr Bropey that he se-mid allow his (Me Brepey'e) name to stand with Mr Thornton' before the constituency until shortly before ths elm:till:a and then withdraw his name and ahoy Mr Henry Thornton a walk-over (" Oh, oh r') Did they ever know of a more barefaced, dishonest and scandalous action than that ? As soon is he (Councillor Tinnion) heard of it, he told Mr Dodds that he had never been a party to anything of a dishonourable nature either it his private or public character, and he would not be a party to anything of the sort he had mentioned He would not sell any ward for anyone else. Re.(C3un- eilllr Tinnion) went ts Mr Thornton, and be it said to . __ . . . . . ...

r :Thornton's honour, he repudiated the whole thing, and said be would not enter the Council by strsh dishon- ourable action. And yet Mr Dodds accused the Liberal party of wirepulling. Mr Dodds had recently joined the Liberal party in Warrington, and he (Councillor Tinnion) went to see him in order to know his position. He told Mr Dodds that he could riot work for the Liberal party and at the flame time work entirely for the non-Trading Committee. Mr DAM had endeavoured to show that he (Councillor Tinnion) wee trying to save an election in St Austin's ward, That was not so. Hs had never been afraid to fieht for his seat on the Town Council. Proceeding to refer to his oppnet- eat (Mr Lord) Councillor Tinnion alluded to the letter which appeared in last Saturday's papers from Mr Lord, and proceeded to detail the conversation he had with Mr Lord. He (Councillor Minion) never stated that the Conservatives were paying Mr Lord's expenees, but he did say that the Municipal Non-Trading Corn. mittee were paying them. Mr Lord told hits that hi- self. Councillor Tinnion also denied that he was one of the 'three and independent sources" inquired of by Mr I John White with referesso to Mr Lord's politics. Why had the non-T rading Committee opposed him (Councillor Tinnion).? Had:he traded to the extent of one halfpenny with the Warrington Cerporatien ? He hod never used his position for one single moment te trade either for himself or for anybody else. Therefore he considered he was a non-trader not only in his words but in his actions. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Tienion referred at considerable length to the inquiry into the aetion of three aldermen by a committee of which he was chairman,and said he was quite prepared to defend tile whole of hi a action in the Council on she non-trading question. He was a non-trader in sympathy. He did not believe in men using their position for their own interests and he was not aware that they had done so. If he saw anything wrong he had sufficient manliness to point it nut without anybody asking him to do so. He bad always striven for purity in public life. He objected to the methods adopted by the Non-Trading Committee. 1 What were those methods ? They were those of whole- sale personal abuse. If Mr Dodds was returned for the Town Hall Ward what would his position be ? He (Councillor Tinnion) con- tended that if Mr Dodds was logical he must admit that what he was about to point Out was immoral trading. Mr Deride was secretary for Messrs Pearsoe and Kuowles Ooal and Iron Campany—s very respectable and highly

cenneoted firm—but if he was a member of the Corpora- tion how could his firm trade with the Corporation as long as he was the paid secretary of the company?At the present time the Corporation had a contract with the company which be (Councillor Tinnion) knew as a mem_ her of the Gas Committee, was for 10,000 or 12,000 tons of fuel in conneotion with the Gas Works. He (Ceuocillor Tinnion) had no fault to find with the contract, but alr Dodds had said that if a man traded, directly or indirectly. with the Corporation he should not be a snlnaber of the Corporation. How, therefore, could he reconcile his present position as • candidate for the Town Hall Ward ? (Applause.) Councillor Tinnion proceeded to refer to the charges of extravag- ance which had neee made against the Comm's Moe. One statement was to the effect that the sum of £7 was spent per week for the use of cabs by officials of the Corporation. That was £350 a year, but the aetual eost of conveyances WVI £461 15' 3d. Those were figures supplied by the Borough Treasurer whose honesty and integrity no one could doubt. (Applause.) Tee large sum he bad named was not spend in the hire of cabs ; a smell proportion was for eabs. The con- veyance of workmen to works in progress cost £lB2 19s. In conneetion with the gas and water works, 'bases were used for takiee moo out to works because they could not get a train there, and if they allowed them to walk sev,ral miles from Warrington there would not only be a lose of time but the men would be tired when they arrived on the job. (Hear, hear.) The removal of fever patients cost £42 161 ; taking five engines to fires £l4 14g. They could not gall a fire engine a cab. (Laughter.) Then there WESI the cost of conveyances for juries to view the bodiee.£l4 ; funerals, and committees visiting works, £3O Us 61. The Water Committe had spent most of the money became° they had had the furthest to go and their ex- I tensions had required most supervision. (Flear, bear.) The coat ire connection with the waterworks was £73 ; in connection with the Watch Committee, and the eon- ' vsyance of prisoners £l7 13s ; School Attendance Com- mittee £7, and there were smaller items in aonneetion with other committees, so that instead of the coet of cabs being £350 it was very much less, because after ' they had deducted the figures he bad quoted there was , ' not much left of the £461 for cabs. (Applause). Mr Dodds had had these figures pointed out to him and had ' promised to have the statement rectified, but nothing had been doer. Dealing with the Hill Warren reservoir, I Councillor Tinnion said it was asserted that the Cor- poration had largely exceeded the estimate. That wee not the case. Tae estimated Celt Was £6,748 and the amount expended was £6,615, so that they s'all had £l3O in hand. Clun- ' oilier Tit:mien next dealt with the statement , that sums amounting to £20,000 had been paid in the names of officials. These payments, he said, were made to officials so that they could pay the wages of the , men. The cheque for the wages of the men at the gas wo-ks was always made out to Mr Taylor, the gos secre- tary, and ha then paid the wages with the money be drew out of the bank. There was nothing wrong about that. Another statement made on hehalf of the Non- Trading Cernmittee was that £30,000 was spent on the Wilderspool tramway. The actual cost was £11,707, and he would leave them to judge of the value of the statements made. Referring to the statement respect ing the erection of poles in Church-street, and their sub- sequent removal, Councillor Tionion said that was another deliberate mis-statement. The poles were erected in the right place in the first instance and had net been removed. (Hear. hear.) In dealing with the personal charges which had been brought against him, Councillor Tinnion said he had never been charged with illegal or immoral trading. He was fighting the ward far purity, and he challenged either Mr Dodds or any 1 member of the Non-Trading Committee to get behind the figures he had quoted that night. They were abso- lutely true and were given on the authority of the Bereueh Treasure?, than whom a more honourable gentleman did not exist. (Hear, hear.) In defending his action with reference to the last election of Alder- men, Councillor 'Bargee said that although certain charges had been ma le against certain aldermen, nothing had been proved. (Hear, hear), With refer- ence to his signing the agreement as to the election of senior councillors for the position of Aldermen,Councillor Tinnion said the time might arrive when this matter ought to he re-e,ensidered.lt was the same resolution that obtained in Manchester and in other towns for the election af aldermen A town councillor who was returned again and again by his sonetituents became the eenior cluneillor, and was it not only fair that the Aldermen should be chosen from those who had given i long service to the town ? (Hear,hear.) He had been I charged with being the cause of the alteration with reference to the sealed tenders ; but if they charged him with tampering with them be would let them know ' what a jury of his own countrymen thought of him. , Re found that tenders eves when sealed with wax, could be tampered with : sealing with wax did not pre- vent that. In some tenders the gum part on she enve- lops had not been wet or aced. That was not sealing. (A Voice : " I say it is.") If sealed with wax a man's own stamp should be used. (Hear, hear). The only Iresolution he moved, after consulting • with the Mayor, was one to the effect that the tenders should be securely fastened or sealed with wax ; if with wax they were to be securely fasteeed. (Fl.ar, bear.) Proceedine to detail what he had done on behalf of St Austin's Ward, Counciller Tinoion asked his hearers to contrast the paving of it at the present time with what it was some years ago. Negotiations had now been cons- pleed for the provision of a playground and steps were also being taken which would lead to the purification of Sankey Brook. (Hear, hear.) In referring to the con- dition of Mill-lase, Councillor Tinnion said if there was one thoroughfare he was therouehly aseamed of, it was Mill-lane. He Was glad to b i in a position to state that the difficulty which arose with Lord Lilford had been settled and the lane would be paved at an early date. Seps were also being taken to improve the lighting of Liverpool-road by the introduction of incandescent lights. (Haar, hear.) With regard to trades uuionisin,he did not think that trade unionitts got that consideration at the hands of the Town Council which they deserved. HP suppnrted the resolution of Counciller Evans's with reference to the right of employees of the Corporation to be rspr 'Rented by their officials in the consideration of grievances. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he said he had given his time ungrudgingly to the services of the town and he appealed to the 2lectors of St. Austin's Ward to give him their stinpron on Saturday next. (Applause.) Mr J ELWELL in moving a resolution to the effect that Councillor Tinnion was. a fit and proper person to repre- sent se Austin's Ward in the town Council, and pledg- ing the meeting to use every effort to secure his return by a large majority,remerked that the base insinuations and false calumny of the non•traders, as they termed themselves, would react against those who used such methods, and they would reap a reward they were not lookinv far. (Hoar, hear.) Mr NATitas CoOK seconded the resolution, and said he should have no hesitation in plumping for Councillor Tinnion. (Applause.) Councillor JAMEI Evans,in the course of an interesting reitroqsect of his work on the Council, referred to the two resolutions which he moved with reference to as iequiry into the trading transactions of the Council. If an inquiry of the kind be advocated had been held, Surely if there had been the rills-spending and illegal trading which they had been told had taken place, the inquiry woul 1 have revealed it. (Hear, bear.) If it had not been for the position taken up towards the pro- posed inquiry by the Municipal.Non-Trading people, he believed the Corporation would have agreed to the inquiry he (Councillor Evans) proposed. If the gentlemen who alleged that these wrong doings had taken place would prove one ef them, he (Councillor Evans) was prepared to take action. Referring to Mr Norbury Williams, Councillor Evans said there were one or two i things mentiened by Mr Williams at Parr Hall to which he valued like to refer, when Mr Williams told his hearers that Warrington was indebted to the extent of one million he did not add that Manchester was indebted to the extent of twenty-eight millions. (" Oh, Oh "). that was up another streeti (Laughter.) Neitner did Mr Williams tell them that Manchester had four millions of unredeemable bonds at four per coat. He would like Mr Williams to say whether that was true or not at the next meeting He (Councillor Evans) had heard on good authority that what he had stated was a fact. With all its blunder- ; hag. Warrington had not been called upon to wash as much dirty linen as Manchester. Warrington bad never been dragged through the mud as Manchester had been with it, police scandals. (Hear, hear). And yet on the authority of Mr Williams, Watrineton was the most corrupt. (Laughter). Referring to Mr Hulme's speeches. Councillor Evans said that gentleman talked a little bit of pretty stuff to amuse the audience. (Laughter). lie , Councillor Evans) believed he could make them laugh as hard as Mr Hulme if he tried —(laughter)—but he would not. Counoiller Erase proceeded to detail the •i interview he had with Mr Charles Lone-

&raw on the pi•ovioos Saturday. e r fußed to sign Cie Municipal Non-Tradiag tia ke Other cal lidstis had no been ask .1 to sign it, and b did not see why he and Councillor Tinnion should be the two speckled birds to be !picked out. (Hear, bear, and laughter-) The only reason for it to his mini was because they were not going to b 3 led. (Hear, hear.) In refering to his action with reference to trade, unionism, Councillor Everss contended than an employe of the Corporation ought to have no diffilulty in getting redress for his grievances. Tho resolution he proposed, . and whieh was aecepted, would assist workraen in that direction. He hod been told that officials of the Cor- onation could transgress with impunity, but be could I assure them that officials would not do it on any con-. mittee on which he had a seat. (Hear, hear.) Counciller Evans proceeded to refer to some of the charges of ex- travagance urged against the Corporation and said there I was one person 14 Warrington who had aiked what did they want with technical school—(Langt.ter)—what did they want with pa-ks P--(laughter)—aal what did I they want with wide streets P (Laughter.) Warring- , ton was a growing and prosperous town and it was the duty of the Corpriatioa to provide for ths social intellectual and physical wants of the inhabitants.

The reselution Was unanimously carried. Clunoillor Wimard ROBERTS then proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman. It was only fair, he slid, that he should take that opportunity of caving one word on the eubjeet of municipal trading. He gave them his solemn assurance that he had never used his position in the Council either directly or indirectly, for the pur- polo of obtaining a half-penny worth et business for any concern he had been connected with. He said that to show how anxious ho was to do right, and he was willing to be judged by those who knew him best. If there was a single meaaber of the Conservative party in the Council who would on the morrow declare that William Roberts had used his position in any shape or form for that purpoq,,he would at Ono, tender his re- signation. He th3ught that was fair. Therefore it was I not fair that he should be branded as a guilty man. What he said of himself was true of others whose names had been dragged through the mire. He had been silent, and others had been silent. beeause he was anxi- ous that the light of day should dawn upon the scandal- ous charges which had been made. He was quite content to wait. The time would come, and it would not be long, when the people of the town would know the truth. What was more cruel than all was this—had that the names of some members of the Town Council been trading as shareholder I of liniti comp tlie3 woo had been purposely withheld from the agitation. Why had his brother had to bear the brunt of all these cruel and wicked attacks? B ?cause he was man enough to stand forward and try to defend himself, and others bad shrank behind his back and allowed him to bear the whole ot the attack, which had been cruel, cowardly and unjust. (Applause.) But the time would come when the truth would be known,and those men—he was one—who bad been unjustly and cruelly accused would have their characters redeemed by the publio opinion of the town. (Applause.) Councillor TINNION seconded the vote af thanks and returned thanks for the vote of confidence in • PAINTERS AND PHYSICIANS.

The meet successful portrait painter is he who over- looks the ugliaeas of his sitter and ye preserves the likeness—never an easy task, and sometimes an impos- sible one from the abseuee of any good feature in the subject. But the work of a nhvsician is mere difficult than that of the painter, for he must not over- look any symptom of his patient, however apparently trivial; and knowing his symptoms exactly must thorouehly cure him of his malady Some physicians reach this high standard, but they are the bright particular stars of their profession, not the rank and file. Fortunately, the multitude of people unable to pay hieh fees, and make special journeys from the provinces to Me Wes. Eire of Lendon,sre not dependent upon thee exceptionally clever men. Every montk for the past thirty-four years thonsands of cases of Indi- gestion and billioueneme have been most effectually cured by Mother BAgere Curative Syrup. Here ig a typical recent cage, that of Mr T H Robssn, master mariner, of 11, Rumney-road, West Eirkdale,Liverpool. " About five years ago," writee Mr Ronson, .. I bad a very trying experience. I suffered severely from con- stipetion and sluggish liver, which took a remarkablY strange turn. The firet indication I kad ef something being seriously wrong with ma was a soreness, nf my limbs. I could net walk without feeling that nay leff• , would give way under me. I grew abnormally stote, and always felt tired and drowsy ; after a meal espsc!- 1 ally, I could have slept for boors. Alarmed at this unnatural conditiea, I consulted a doctor, solo thought at first that rey trouble was occasioned by fiatulescy ; but after a time, as I went from rad to worse, he gave me a letter for an infirmary. where I was examined by three doctors, wig. decided that my case was one of flatulency and aerv."ii prostration, intensified by mental worry. TheY advise _ ma to go away for a change of same, and to cease worrying. After being twice tapped for dropsy. and experincing only temporary relief, I was for a while at a loss what to do for to best, when one day it occurred to me to try Mother Seigel' Curative Syrup. and I aslod my wife to get me a bottle ot i. It proved • lucky thnught, for my constitution, which bad resisted all preview treatment, yielded at once. By the time I bad taken three bottles, my clothes, which for a lost time I had fastened with difficulty, hung loose upon me• I have undergone no further operation, and my health, has singe been as satisfactory as I could wish it to be. TESTIMONIAL TO AN EARLESTOWN INSPECTOR.

At the Newton Police Court on Thursday morning Inspector Morgan, the late inspector for the Earlestows and Newton Police District, was presented with illuminated address, and a purse of gold, in recognition of his services. The presentation was made by Mr T J ! Gillespie (chairman),who was accompanied on the bench by Messrs J W Emmett and J Unsworth and Dr DrA'' ling, and there were also present amongst a crowded audience the Revs T It Mathews and J C Matthews, Dr 1 J N Patterson, Superintcadent Coker, Slessri A E Browne, Artialir Smith, T Bowes, T Siddeley, Is% Inspector Morgan, who is now at Lytham, thanked Mr Gillespie for the kind words he had spoken. Re I thanked Mr B3wes and Mr Siddeley (the eecretariee), Dr Pattereen (the treasurer), and said he had always re- ceived the utmost courtesy from the bench, the magis- trates' clerk, s dicitors, and police officials, and the testimonial would keep him in mind of the old time. (Applause.) The tes'imonial reads :—" To Police-Inspector John Morgaa,who for the past eight years has been Inspector ot Police in charge of the Newton Sub-Division of War- rington Police Division of the County of Lancaster, and who, during that time has,with unvarying kindness and consideration to the inhabitants of th:e township, in the discharge of his onerous duties, and by his zeal in the promotion of every good cause for the well-being and benefit of the said inhabitants, gained the respect and esteem of all who have come into contact with hien. This testimonial, together with a purse of gold, contain- ing fifty sovereigns, presented te him he his many friends Ore his leaving thie di3trict (by medical advise) to take up hie duties at Lytham, is a :oken of the regre and high esteem in which be was held." e The testineoniel was signed by the committee, with the Rev T R Matthews (chairman), Dr J N Paterson (treasurer), and Messrs Thomas Bowes rind Thomas Siddeley (secretaries).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
LEIGH "A " v WARRINGTON A."

This match took place at Leigh on Saturday. Leigh showe4 'etter combination from the outset: From a scrim- mage, Hinson obtained and dodged over Ramidale failed at goal. Then Meacock lost possession on his own line, and Collins, following on well scared. Rainsdale failed to augment. From a penalty Ramadale landed a capital goal. At the interval Leigh led by eight points to nil. In the second half. Hinson passed to Barr. who made a capital attempt to score. Brooks tackling him on the line- Just before time Stout scored an unimproved try. Final : Leigh. one goal three tries (II points) ; Warrington. nil. LANCASHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE.

Played at Latchford. During the first half Bate scered for Latchford who pressed continually, the visitors' defence hav- ing all their work cut out to prevent further scoring. half time Latchford Rangers. three points ; Widnes Rangers. nil. In the second half Hallam was conspicuous for some fine play, keeping his lines clear, Latchford gained ground and from a scrum Bate got possession and passed to Flem- ing, who scored at the corner flag, the goal kick failing. The home forwards were soon again on the visitors' lines, when they were awarded a penalty. Brown k.cking the goal. Final Latchford Rangers, eight points; Widnes Rangers nil.

,There is no doubt that we Hire in an age of worry and excitement, and as the struggle for existence is anything but conducive to good digestion or an appetite that can relish anything, the palate of the average work.a.day individual has to be tickled and tempted in a variety of ways. We are often lectured about the evil effects of an over.indulgence in tea or eofiee, not to mention intoxicating liquors, until many people are bewildered what to turn to for a beverage which shall be at once agreeable to the taste and supply the desired nourishing and stimulating qualities. Public attention has been freely drawn to the merits of Or. Insurance Dispute :at Warrington.

At the Police Court, on Friday, Mary E Kinsella 4, Halitex-street, claimed ten guineas under a life policy in the National Guardian Assurance Com- pany on her son Thomas Kinsella, who died on August 15, 1902.—Mr Steel, who appeared for the plaintiff, said Mrs Kinsella was a widow and the action was taken against John Stephens. Legh- street, who was the agent for the company. The last payment was made by Mrs Kinsella on April 7 of this year, and the agency was afterwards changed. Mrs Kinsella did not know that there was any office in the town, and she told a neighbour to request the ~;agent to call at her house, but no agent ever did until after the death of her son which oc- curred on August 15. On the week following Mr Stephens called upon her,and asked for her policies and after some trouble, she found seven, where- upon he took them away with him. She heard no more of him, but quite by accident she met him. After some time she got six policies back. The matter was put into his (Mr Steel's) hands, and a claim for ten guineas was made, but a reply was received that notice of lapse had been served and, therefore, there was no liability. No notice had, however, been served. He contended that this was a mean way of getting out of the liability to pay, as it was not Mrs Kinsella's fault that the premiums had not been paid,— Mr Riley, for the defence, said the company was in liquidation, and the petition had been filed on August 1 of the present year, The present proceed- ings were therefore useless:—The ease was after- wards withdrawn by Mr Steel. Further action will be taken

Warrington Meld Club. A meeting of this club was held in the Museum Lecture Room last night week, Mr Womenley pre- siding. Mr W Webster read a paper on "A Holi- day in Wales." He described, some of the scenic features of Mid-Wales. and related some of his experiences as a collector and observer. His special subjects, ants and spiders, are not commonly regar- ded as attractive, but he was able to enlist the sympathies of his hearers with both. It was agreed by the courtesy of the Museum Sub-Com- mittee, to have a joint meeting with the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Entomological Society in the Lecture Room on December Bth.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND. ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND. ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By Ovalist.]

My confidence in Warrington was not misplaced on 'Saturday, for with such absentees as Fish, Harris, and Boardman, the homesters proved too good for Leigh. That the 'atter thought they had a" sweet thing" with both Warrington's wings playing for the County cannot be denied, but there is many a slip, Sm., as the visitors soon discovered. Warrington's performance was one which does them infinite credit, proving moreover that the team does not lack resource•and pluck. The brand- new jerseys may have stimulated them to greater exertions—at any rate, they smartened the men up con- siderably and made the fifteen look more like an up-to- date combination than an assortment of tin-can chasers, which they resembled on more than one occasion last season when the stock of apparel had got low. Needless to say. the crowd was as pleased on Saturday with the appearance of the men as with the smart performance they gave.

There was some fear that Dickenson would also be called upon to assist the County, but, fortunately R Wilson turned up and the lengthy Warring,tonian assisted his native club. I was of the opinion before the match that our halves and centres alone were good enough to win the game, and that opinion was con- firmed before the close, for it was undoubtedly the fine combination and dash of these four that broke down the Leigh defence every time. They played superbly, and with two such good wings alongside at Fish and Harris, they must have given the visitors a most severe handling. As it was Leigh got much more than they bargained for, as the score of 1 goal 3 tries to 3 goals 1 try shows.

--N- Flomq matches just now are rare at Warrington, and there was a fine crowd at Wilderspool to see the locals for the third time only this season. Leigh were also well supported, the prospect of a victory bringing many of the Mather-lane enthusiasts. Leigh started off in a style which boded ill for the homesters,and had Neville scored from the mis-catch by Edmunds on the line, Warrington might have had a difficult task to get the upper hand. The lengthy winger fell in his eagerness I however, and "little Tich " made no more mistakes that afternoon. Leigh were the first to score as it was, Dunbavin dropping the usual goal the first time he got within range. Lusty shouts and sarcastic remarks about the fate of Warrington were heard on every side where Leigh men congregated. But Warrington were only just getting used to the" feel" of the new jerseys, and they presently made things hum. Leigh had to defend, and in a trice a brilliant piece of work by the home halves and centres resulted in Forster scoring a try at the corner. Leigh immediately got to the other end through a mistake by Knight,and Dunbavin made a drop for goal from short range. Knight charged at the same moment and not only deflected the flight of the ball but upset the droppist, ho was hurt and left the field. Warrington still led by a try to a goal at half-time.

• Dunbavin pluckily returned after the interval and though lame he lowered the home goal a second time with a magnificent drop kick quite 40 yards out. This only served to brace Warrington up again, and they completely over-played Leigh fore and aft. Dickenson ran over in brilliant style after fine passing, Pearson having no chance with either the scorer or Forster who was in attendance. This appeared to settle matters and Dunb•vin retired finally. Isherwood soon after- wards scored behind the posts and kicked a goal, and it only seemed a question of Warrington's margin when Neville intercepted a pass at centre and outpacing everybody, gained a try for Leigh, which Johnson con- verted, and Warrington were only two points ahead. Leigh made desperate efforts after this but were driven back and Warrington won:an exciting game.by eleven points to nine points.

Though Leigh have done well this season they still lack finish in the rear division, the halves being the only class exponents, and they are too much addicted to drop kicking. Warrington's combination, and quick, short passing were too much for the Leigh backs, who got an admirable lesson in the way to score tries. Edmunds and Forster on the wing played finely for Warrington, and deserved the hearty cheers they fre- quently got, but as I have said already the halves and centres were the means of winning the game, and their form was such as to bode ill for some of the clubs , Warrington have yet to meet. Ido like the way they dash straight down the centre instead of running to- wards touch, and these effective tactics should bring plenty of points this season. Knight was unreliable and, indeed, seems to play his worst games at home. The forwards played a grand game, Morrison being noticeably prominent Molyneux and Pearson were the best men on the Leigh side, the threequarters having little idea of combination and less opportunity. Under fair conditions I think Warrington will take four points out of the Mather-laners this season.
Salford, Oldham, and Swinton were all among the vanquished last Saturday, Halifax and Runcorn being still the undefeated ones. The former have still kept their line intact.
