div.head: THE
div.p: THE
EDUCATION BILL
ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING in Parr Hall.
Scathing Criticism of the,. Measure. Speech by Mr.Broadhurst, M.P.

A great demonstration against the Education Bill was held at Warrington on Tuesday evening, under the auspices of the Liberal Association, the Women's Liberal Association, and the Free Church Council. Parr Hall was well filled, and there was much enthusiasm. Mr Henry Broadhurst, M.P., was the principal speaker, supported by Mr C Nicholson (Liberal candidates for Doncaster division). Mr Charles Parker presided. kir BROADHURST M.P., who was received with pro- longed applause, said that one of the chief reasons why be. as a working man ,took such a deep interest in the education question WAS due to the fact that having been born in a rural village sixty years ago, when there were no School Boards,educatioa was indeed difficult for pocr children to obtain—even a fair smattering ot elementary education. Sicco then to the present lime he had been working on an average 13 to 14 hours a day so that the evening contieuation schools initi- ated by the School Boar I had been of very little &rvice to him. Having experienced at many stages of his life and still experiencing daily his lack of education and the fearful defect created by want of educational opportunities in early life, he adv eated and worked for tee placing within the reach of every man and child the best educatien posaible to give them. (Applause.) They should and ought to have opportunity. And if the child had a natural capacity he should have the chance of using that opportunity to the benefit of himself, his family, and the nation at large. That was his introduction to the educational die- pute that was occupying the attention of the country to the exclusion of all other subjects. In so far as it did that it would do good. There was no question in his judgment of a social !salute, half so important to their country, their empire, and their people at home as the future brain and moral power of the men and women of that which was the centre of their empire— (applause)—and the beehive of the industrial world. (Renewed applause.) At the present moment they were undoubtedly passing through a great and serious crisis. Tne Chairman in his masterly and dissecting speech had notlen the least over-estimated its importance. They had is Bill of between twenty and thirty clauses in the 26use of Commons, and they were only just through e first paragraph of clause 8 after many months of debate on the subject.lt had been fought not only clause by clause but line by line and word by word, not in the interest of any party or faction or as a pclitical move in the great work of the elation, but it bad been fought by men conscious of the enor- mous responsibility resting upon them and determined to do all that lay in their power not to improve—ne ! the day was passed fur improvement—(applause)—there was no such thing as mending the bill with any satis- faction to the opinions of the people or to the advan- tage of education • The only thing that could be use- fully done tolit—if that were possible—was not to mend it but to end 'it. (Loud applause.) Mending it was impossible. The very foundation of the bill was wrong the whole conception of it was wirong—Wreng from the first line on the first page to the last lice on the last sheet. (fleet, hear.) That was his opinion of the bill. Ho toad been asked to give them hie opinion and be gave it without prejudice. (Applause.) On Mcnday afternoon from two o'clock to 7.30 they were discussing as te whether and under what conditions the management should be permitted to dis- charge a teacher w'thout approval or consultation with the local authority. He wished his fellow workers to follow this thought as well as they could. The local authority and the areas of the local authority would mean in their case the Town Council, as in the case of all other boroughs. The local authority in counties would mean the County Council. The management would be largely, and probably in nine cases out of ten. wholly in spirit and in practice the management of the present men and women—especially in the case of rural voluntary schools. That was a dis- tinct explanation of areas, which it was important to observe in the discussion of a subject se confused in many respects as was the subject of the bill. He wished to be allowed to state his position on the education question. When he said his position he meant the position of many every Liberal member in the House of Com- mons, and probably the opinion of the greater part of Free Church worshippers and ministers even in W4r- rington. (Applause). His opinion was that the great— nay sacred—cause awl work of training the brains and the moral character of their future *men and women was so transcendently important that it ought not to be even suspected to be under the control of any section, of any churl), or any particular religious denomination. (Applause). Its duty should be discharged by the State, and paid for by the State. (Hear, hear.) The State was the people. And therefore the State. in other words the people, should directly control and manage their own schools in their own particular area. Do not let anyone think or say that he was advocating a pure and simple seeulsr education. He did not forget the religious character of their children which it should be their duty to endeavour to form. Surely any man or women who had gone through his college training for the high work of teaching and obtained his or her parchment—the certificate of proficiency for that work—must be and were capable of laying down the elementary principles of religion as taught in the New Testament. Any man or woman who could not do that was not fit for the work of teaching the child. i (Applause). Such work could be done to the satisfac- tion of all reasonable and fair minded people. Thus there could be implanted into the young mind from its early tottering years of 5 to 15 great principle& And in the home life and the Sunday school of each denomina- tion could be added to what the child gained in the day schools, such particular views as met wita the approval. of the household in which the child resided If he had not been lucid enough on the point let him have the beeefit of it. He repeated that he believed in religious education in every elementary school that would satisfy all reason and offend no susceptibility. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that was a reasonable and fair proposition. (Applause). If they could arrive at such a conclusion they could then proceed with the other branches of e lsmentary teechine. U ow the present Bill went,as near as oossible,in exactly the opposite direction. (Hear. hear). That was why he objected to the Bill. He objected to its foundation to start with. He objected to the great and all important question of education being handed over to Town Councils and the County Council. He believed in what the scholars called the ad hoc principle. He believed in bodies elected for that opecific purpose, and that purpose only. (Applause.) Look at their Town Council! (Slight laughter.) He had forgotten. He did not want to point out any specific Council. (Laughter.) It was Councils he was dealing with. Well ! all over the country the work of the Town Councils was increasing year by year. They had as much work as they could find time to get through. And the difficulty in their own town, and in other towns and cities was to get the right class of men to serve the burgesses—(applause)—on account of the enormous amount of time occupied by Council work. Then of all things to add education was the last thing that any man knowing anything of the condition of municipal life would ever have thrown down in their midst to be wrangled over. Tae County Councils were the same. The County Councils se far as his experience of of them went were almost overloaded already with County work. He spoke as an Alderman of a County Council of a great many years standing. Yet they were going to add to the work a ' question which divided men almost more than any other question—that of education. He did not like to speak aisregpectfully of anyone, but he could not think that any minister who had the faintest elementary knowledge ' of county add borough life could ever have been induced to draw up such a Bill as the one they were discussing. In his own county he bad to leave his cottage ern?' in the morning and bad te travel 50 miles before getting to the County Council meeting. And this showed conclusively that though the County Council was elected on popular suffrage in one respect the membership was limited be- cause only those could be members; who could afford to lose a day's work and pay the train fare,maybe a matter of 10a,and the out-of-pocket expenses of the day. How could that be a popular body? (Applause.) The member ship was limited not by a property qualification, or statute law, but by a property qualification in practice. .Yet the other side told them it was a measure to be admin- istered by the great oracularly elected public authorities of the country. It did not follow that a man who was an authority on agricultural matters was also the best in the matter of education. The chances were that he was not, but exactly the contrary. (Hear, bear.) Sir John Gorst had admitted that the farmer and the squire were no friends of elementary education. They were opposed to teaching which gave the children wings with which to fly cut of the parish. How could the labourer he educated when every element surrounding him was opposed to it? He could not explain at once his funda- mental objections to the Bill. They could quite under- stand be could not do in one hour what the House of Commons had failed to do in three months. The prin- cipal thing, however, was that they wanted the education to be levelled up and not down. (Hear, hear.) The Bill undoubtedly had a ten- deney—and in his firm opinion would in practice level down instead of levelling up. The outcome of the bill from previous experience might lead them astray. .1. great many weak-kneed Nonconformite were saying they acknowledged and thanked the Church for what she had done for elementary education. He acknow- ledged nrthing of the hind. (Applause.) In UN the floia.se of Commons passed a Bill which would have

given practically a School Board in every parish in the kingdom controlled by the people. Who defeated the Bill ? The ecclesiastical elemtinte in the Hones of Lords. , (Shame.) Instead of thanking them he believed them I responsible for the century of strife and neglect of ele- mentary edecation. (Applause.) Not oely had they n, thing to thank them for, but the nation had .cause to regret the presence in Parliament :n the Uppf r House of those elements which were able to thwart and destroy a measure which would have made the country one hundred years in advance of what it was at the preseat day. Yea ! Voluntaryism was begotten of a fear of popu- larisni. He would withdraw that statement. Be would not impute motivee,which was a dangerous thing to de. But they might draw a conclusion in that direction without making the raw ariseetioa. So mach for their thanks to the church— le meant, of course the Govern- ment Cnurch, the State Cnurch, the Church of England eetieteliehed and controlled by law—when the law breakers were not too strong for tiee Bishop and he got afraid of them. (Laughter and applause.) Before coming to that meeting a pamphlet had been sent to hi rn written by the Rev Mr Dyinott, aLivpool vicar. Among other statements was one wake said that th voruntary schools gave the same education as Beard schools. There was not another man in Et:gland who would make such an assertion. Facts were against the statement—against eerryboly who made Tech rash unwarrantable and untruthful aesnitiene. In nothing were the v. 'watery schools as good as the Board seinots. Fortunately for them—poor ignorant benighted Non- conformist opponents of the Bill—they had John Gorst's speech delivesecl as educational minister to use when referring to the country life objections to elementary education. He gave them a rare illu- stration of the efficieney of the vnluntary system. The statistics of London, Live-peel, and Maischester showed that the scholarships won by the scholars of the secterian schools, they were sectarian net voluntary when 163 or 175 were paid out of every from the taxes (shame) were only 30 while those won by the Board were 350. (Applause). The number propor- tionately that should have b-,en won by the sectarian schools was 180 instead of 30 so that they were 150 behind. How coule it be said that the teaching was the same in the yolunt try school as in the Board School ? If they went to their music or cookery classes or the like they would find that the sectarian schools were far behind the Board schools. Yet the Bill di- strayed the the system and set up in its place inefficiency. (Applause). Clause 7 had passed arid part of thew 8, and there was to be a majority of 4 agaiust 2 in every management of all the state schools in the country. (Shame). They (the ratepayers) were to live in a per- petual minority of two. There was also ne guarantee that the minority of 2 would not be exactly of the same class of opinions as the majority of 4. (Applause). There was no provision in the Bill to the contrarr. How then were they going to have any control at all over the education of their children? How could the authority then control the management? It might do on paper but would it in practice ? (Ace- plause.) Of course it would not. A deal had been said atieat the want of religious instruction in the Beard school. It had been called " Godless education," " A sort of religious edacation " and " leio religious educa- tion at all." What did Sir John Gorst say in the speech referred to ? Quoting from Hansard he found him rav- ing" I was speaking in the House some little time ago when I expressed my doubts whether the teaching of the historical facts of religion was given better in Board schools than in Veluntery echo es. I enteetain that doubt no longer. In London at any rate I have no hesitatioa in saying that the teaching in Board schools is so superior to the teaching in Voluntary schools that there is no comparison between them." What about Godless education ? The diocesan inspectors were fall of lamentation over the inefficiency of religious education in the Church schools. In some cases no religious educa- tion had been given for weeks, because they were try- ing to cavil the children for soma other subjects for examination. In some schools there were no Bibles. Had they ever heard of a Board school without a Bible ? There was not even a common prayer book. (Hear, hear.) Every authority was against the alleged ineffi- ciency of Beard religious instruction in spite of the Doan of St Faille. If Nonconformists were to make such statements about the church he knew the language that would be employed. But the Nonconformists had to set good examples. (Laughter.) They respected them- selves and the connections with which they were asso- ciated. What class of men were to have the manage- ment of the schools? Some as good as ever walked. (Applause.) In the service ef the Church of England he had a few who permitte,d him to call them his friends—men of whose honour there was neither doubt nor question, whose minds were ae broad as the ocean. He had had the privilege of friend- ship with bishops. (Laughter.) Archbishop Lait was one of the finest men he bad ever met, liberal to a degree in all his dealings with every class of people. But mese were the •xoeptlous. They had to I deal with present facts. Were they going to hand their children over in every case to men who no longer preached the protestant religion. (Applause.) He accorded to every man living the same freedom in religious matters as be demanded for himself. (Applause.) He reenacted and honoured the Roman Catholic. But he disliked the wolf in sheep's clothing. (Applause.)—tee man who accepted Protestant emolu- ments and position, and practised dectrine directly (versed to that for which he was paid for teaching. The day previous he listened to a letter read by Dr Macnamera—that master of the education question. Be had never heard such a production in all his life before. Among other things in the letter the teacher was asked by the Vicar whether he was an early and fre- quent communicant, whether he played the organ. Must be a good Catholic ? Not a single word about education for which the State was going to pay. These were the men who were to , manage the elementary school and control the children of the Nonconformist. He did not know whether he had exhausted all the duties expected of him. (Laugh- ter.) But there might have been other menial duties be would have to perform. (It Voice : "Sweep out the church.") (Laughter.) If it could be swept out the better for the Church of England. (Applause.) In the case of Fireiponde, near Bristol out of a voluntary school income of £559, 1512 were from the State. At the school, boys bad beau caned for not attending the ritual- istic lecture to which the parents if of Nonconformists , and Protestant children objected to send their children. He had recently seen an advertirement which ran : " Headmaster required for school. lie most be a thorough Catholic"—this was from a Voluntary Church school-6' lie must leach the faith and formularies. Ne other need apply." At the present time they had 1,700 unqualified teachers proffesing te teach children when they never successfully passed their own examinations. The present Bill would perpetuate the present state of affeirs. Were they going to give them an untimi'ed run upon their taxes without any efficient • control PI If they did they could look forward to the worst days of Catholicism in the country- And they would betray the liberties and freedom of conscience won for them by their father,. Were they going to stand it ? (No, no ) He would not ask them to disobey the law. But if the Bill were passed it would load to scenes that all would I regret, and many would suffer. It was hard to force a person to pay for propagating religious tenets he did not agree with. Thousands of Churchmen °elect id to the Bill, and they did not want to prets the Bill home. , In conclusion he appealed to his fell ave workers to stand firm. If the 13i1l b mime law, out with every in m who voted for it. (Amelauee). Never mind politics. (Hear, hear,) The spiritual life, the freedom and the unwarped intelligence of childhood were of far more value than all political parties put together. (Applause). The greatest rower in the world was knowledge. (Hear, hear.) They could only have accurate knowledge by sound elementary educaticat ; they would only hive sound, high-Maas intellectual results by haying the beet I men and women that money could buy to teach their I children. A teacher who had to submit to a dogmatic test in religion in order to obtain an appointment, and who had to mak a declara- tion of a faith which he or she had not sub- scribed to, became an immoral man or woman, an-I I was totally unfit to bring up the cnildren of tha people —(applause)—and he who imposed the test and seduced or enticed the teacher from the faith which he or she held was a greater traitor and more immoral than the teacher who succumbed. (Hear, hat.) They most gfj.) to it that they had their training colleges sufficient in number and accommodation and equipment to train a staff of men and women who would impart to tie chil- dren of this country, discipline, respect, faith, truth, knowledge, and moral strength. (Applause.) Let the ecclesiastics keep within their own sphere and the public would respect them. He (Mr Broadhurst) never showed the least want of respect to any professed teacher of religion so long as h 3 kept off his (Mr Broadhurstes) feet and his bands out of his (Mr BroadhursCs) pocket (Applause.) He would ask all present to stand by the education of their children and let nothing into, vene be- tween therm and the acquisition of knowledge. (Hear, hear.) Ile should continue to fight age inst the Bill. He regretted he was even away for those few hours that night. He should not be surprised to see the Bill receive the Royal assent before Christmas, and if it did then the public were unworthy of the liberty they at present enjoyed if they did not oust every man out of the House of Commons who had voted for it. (Applause.) He would not demur if they elected a Parliament with a mandate on the one subject of education, and enabled them to settle the question on a basis that would enable U 9 to fight the nations of the world in intellectual Means of production. (Applause.) He appealed to the audience to pass the resolution which was to be submitted, with enthusiasm. (Applause.)

The circum- , stances that called for the resolution, he l said, ought never to have existed in a I land so famous for religious freedom. (Hear, hear). ' It was one of the unfortunate signs of the present crisis that if a man dared to oppose the Bill which was being forced through Perlianient, he was liable to be charged , with misrepresentation, his motives impugned, his con- science saeered at, arid called a political agitator. A more unfortunate Bill could scarcely have b ten intro- , duced ta mar the year of the King's coronation and the year of the peace rejoicinge. (Beer, hear.) It coatained so nuch that was offensive to the principles of the Free Churches and was apparently designed to check 'he onward m irch of Nonconformity by a Hered-like policy / of making havoc of their children. It would be a strange thiog Indeed, if as representatives of the Free Churches thee sat down quietly, shut their eyes retro opened their mouths, and submissively swallowed what the Siebert a in convocation, the Efigh Church party and the II -man hiererchy, had so considerately prepared behin I their backs. Newer.- formises bad too much vitality to b I put out of exist- ence in that way and they laced their children too well to leave their religious training to the priests. The present Bill was an attempt to kill tee sehool boards because they were a more effective instrument of e he- , cation, than sectarian'enstituzions. As Nonconformists they indignantly denied the charge that they hod , neelected the education of their children. If their names had not been distinctly aisecieted with day schoe s it WAS beceuse they believed it to he the duty of the S ate to supply all children with a good, sound, secular education, and the duty of the chufc les to look after their religion/ tr. defog. (Apelarese ) Ii tear prin- ciple had been fought to its issue in 1870 instead Of the , compromise which hod now been thrown to the winds, there would be no religious difficu ty to puzzle politicians and embroil the nation. But so ling as the State put forth its hand into thsen long wnalo Lite, il heatsuer tle ttaot ,: endowoe rpwsect- arian iitetitutioes, o the re Woos eifficulty, ,trif 3 and barer/vele, (gee:, / hear.) fhe Governinani'i Bull took away their riot, to , elect school boards where they had a chance of on occa- sional majerity. It reduced any control to I a minimum. It perpetuated sectarian bitterness, it put more sterol), in the cleric and the squire an I made it / more difficult for the village Noncentormist. And this Il was the Bill which was proclaimed as fair, equitable.,and I just ! They would be unworthy of the position they held and of the traditions they loved, and of the brave fathers who fought so noloey for their libertiee, if they / submitted to such a ore-aided arrangement. (Applause.) 1 Through the federation of their Free Churches they stood in unbroken ranks and with one voice condemned this Bill. They were determined to do what they could to / defeat he aims and frustrate its purposes and some of them were ready to stake the spoiling of their glees I rather than submit to so unj oat, unconscicutional and reactionary a ,measure. (Applause.) . Mrs ROBERT GrARNETT seconded the resolution. She had hopeo that there worild have been no necessity for 1 her to speak that evening, but she had been asked to raise her voice as a woman against the measure, because by the Bill, women would be disqualified from , acting on School Boards. From the promise of Mr , Ritchie and tine letter which Mr Balfour had addressed to , a correspondent, they might really assume that the I Government did recognise the desirability of avoiding I such a disaster to the country as would be sure to follow the exclusion of women who had served their country , so well for 30 years from continuing to do so with regard to the education of the country. (Hear, hear.) Fully one-half of the children in our schools were females and at least oae-balf of the teacners were females. (Hear, hear-) She could not believe that with a mother like Mr Balfour had had, he could ever have intended to exclude women from well a position, since he owed so ' much to the religious education imparted to him by Lady Balfour. Perhaps it was one of those unpleasant corollories which followed in the wake of legislation that the Act which would sweep away Board Schools, would cut off 260 women from serving on Scheel Boards as they had hitherto done. It was for that purpose she wag asked to speak, and she did so in behalf of that par- ticular item in the 8.11. She did not profess to under- stand this very unmanageable and more isonable Bill— and she had never found anyone really able to master it (laughter)—so that she need not apologise for not being able to understand it. (Hear, hear.) In its action as regarded women she protested against the Bill, and she had much p:easure in seconding the resolution. )Applause). The resolution was thee put to the meeting and carried with enthusiasm. A few nande were held np against the resolution, the Criainteate remarking that there were no; more than six at the outside. Mr Charles NIOIIOVON, who was introduced as the son-in-law of the late very much eSspactscl Ste CkkOrgd Croenere. then addressed the 'mooting. Be said it was almost 21. years to a day since be stood on a political ielatform in Warringten. On that occasion his late father-in-law was in the chair and Mr John Crosfield was also present. They had a most enthusiastic meeting which ended in a torch-light processicn half the way home. It was staled in support of the candidature of the late Mr McMinnies. He forgot who his opponent Was but it Was probably a brewer. (Laughter.) The incident that remained most forcibly in his mind was 1 the glorin.us speech of Mr Peter Relands. Waving his hand over his head, Mr Peter Rylands said he knew who was going to win. And Mr Rylands WM right. Be (Mr , Nicholson) wished he could be as certain that Mr Arthur I Crosfield was going to win in the coming battle as Mr I Peter Rylands was that Mr McAlinnies would. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the Bill Mr Nicholson said he did , not stand there as the representative or partisan of any particular creed whatever. It was not a quarrel between i church and chapel ; nor did the Nonconformists begin the fight. They had been forced into this battle and had I been bound to take up the position they now stood in. ! (Hear, hear.) Nor was this a battle between political parties in the ordinary sense of the term. They would find strong hereditary Conservatives objecting to , certain orinciplee in this Bill. And what about the Liberal Unionists? They all knew how Mr Chamberlain went down to the conference of Unionist prepared to quell the opposition to the Bill. He spoke the whole time so that nobody could object—a very simple way of managing a meeting which was likely to be objectioe- able. (Laughter). Mr Chamberlain told them that if the Bill did not pass, the Government would resign and if it did resign, the government of the country would be put haok into the hands of the prn-Boers, the little Englanders and the Home Rulers. (f.aughter.) Mr Chamberlain himself was relying on Cardinal Vaughan and the Irish party to carry this Bill through. It did not lie irt his mouth to taunt the Liberals with coquetting with the Irish party. (Hear, hear.) What was the claim of I Ulla church in this matter ? Tney said 1 that during the last 100 years they had spent £40,000 000 in private schools for educating children. There was considerable diffireoce as to the amount. He noticed that a week or two beck, after some investiga- tion, the church party put the vs lute of the schools as high as £120.000.000, On the other hand, Sir William fla, court had put the value at £15,000.000. Let them estimate that the schools had cost £40,000,000. Ile contended that the money had not been given exclu- sively by Church people. There were many pemple un- connected with the Church of England woo in the early days of the movement felt it to be a patriotic duty to assist education and who tnerefore subscribed towards the erection of the schools. (Hear, hear.) Be should say that half the people who gave the church this £40,000,000 were of that sort. The Government were spending money at the rate of £12,000,000 a year on the cost of education. In four years time the Government would have spent more than the church had anent in 100 years (Hear, hear) The church said what about our grievances ? For years past we have had to find the cost of /our voluntary schools and in addition we have had to pay taxes for the support of Board schools which we don't believe in. That was a more monstrous claim than the other.(Hesr, hear ) The Board schools were as much their schools as anyone else's. He had never known a School Board. election which the church had not taken an interest in 'Caere wer e many clergymen whol sat on School Boards and they were perfectly right and justified in doing so if chosen by the electorate, but to say that because they haven't managed to capture the whole of the School Board system that therefore the cost of their schools bad to be made over to them was a moestrous claim. ;App'aese.) What was the claim of the nation? It was that each child should have the very best educa- tion that money could buy. (Hear, hear.) There was not a sinels subject of examination in which the Board children,e ch oel ch ei lvd(r? ne Ili nwtehries nvoetrya h tehaied o ol of gti chae l knowledge Voluntary which School the Voluntary school manaeers set themselves to teach. In general knowledge the Board School children were 22 per cent ahead of the Voluntary School children ; in 1 infant instructioe the Beard School children were 28 per cent ahead ; in singing 11 per cent ahead e. in general efficiency 17 per cent ahead. (Applause.) At the pre- s.nt time the nation was paying 81 per cent of the cost of voluntary schools and getting no control at all for the money. Referring to the teaching profession, Mr i Nicholson Bahl that was in mans respects the noblest I profession we had. There were 44 training colleges in this country and only eight of these were undenomi- national. The pressure on these,as they could naturally understand, was very great. A pupil teacher having gone round and found the undenominational colleges fell, turned to the Church of England colleges and the first question put to the candidate for admission was " Are you a communicant of the Church of Eng- land? " The first thing that was likely to happen was to mace the pupil teacher abjure the faith of his father and become Npheretic or else they would be shutting the door against the pupil teacher who would not change his faith in order to eain adtnission. Was it right that 1 the teaching profession should remain simply a preserve I for the Anglican church ; was it right that over the door of the entrance there should in effect be the words " No , Nonconformist need apply."? (Applause). Our educa- , tional system lead been allowed to get behind the times. 1 Germany and America were ahead of us and we had get 1 Ito make that up. (Hear, hear). For that reason he ‘, Said, the teaching profession should be thrown open to I all. There should be no theological tests, the only taet

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: THE RESOLUTION.

• The Rev J S HUGHES moved the following resolution : That this meeting of inhabitants of Warrington, convened by the Warrington Liberal Association ; the Liberal Women's Association ; and the Warrington and District Free Church Council, desires to plane on record, its emphatic protest against the Education Bill now be- fore Parliament. because :—First : That it contravenes religious equality, by compelling children, in many cases, to find education in denominational schools with- out any adequate security from religious teaching to which parents object, and by barring the entrance to schools and training colleges by religious tests. Second : That it repudiateethat right of direct pepular control

b..? ability to teach and vod character. (H?ar hear). In concuasion, Nicholson referred to the' criticisms which hAd hien passed on the onpinents of the Education Bill and said the taunts which bad been made were unjustified and uncalliid,for. (Applause).

A sensational case was disclosed in the Southwark Police Court; oa do ad iv when G:eorg Chapman, the landlord or ti s C,own public-hoass,Barou?,h Eli,th-s;teet a few do zs from 8; Ge)rg Clurc Wi9 charged with the wilful murder of Maud Marsh (a girl of 20), who had been employed as a barmaid at the Crown or sonic nine naonths, and had live i with the puntiean as his. wife), by poisoning her with arsenic.

At a quarter past tin that night Gadley sew Chap- man in the station. " From inquiries I have made," he tcli the prisoner, "it is now my ,iuty to charge you with toe wilful murder of Mau I Marsh." "I am innocent," Chapman answered, and askellt if he could have bail. But the Inspector refused. •• When did the woman (lit? ' the magistrate asked. " On 'he 22cd of this month, at the prisoner's resid- encl," the inspector replied. " I my add, sir, that tram inquiries I have made it seems that Chapman was the only person win gave her her food. He woun not ad )vz anyone to be in the kitchen wialle he prepared it. And this is the third woman who has died in his house witnin t..e past five years." Then, unwrapping a brown pap ,r parcel he had with him, Mr Godley added : " I found these five medical books, all on medicine, in the prisonor's possession, as well as some white powders, which have not yet been analysed." It happened that the doctor called in to see Maud Marsh, had also been called in to see another woman who had died in one of Chapinan's houses, sod noticingim I.)r symptoms, his suspicions wpro am ,used, and he now stated that this nest woman who had died at tho Monument public- house, Union-streer, had been pcwoned too. Followingupon the mystei:ous death of Maud Marsh, the Southwark barmaid,it is stated that the Horne Secre- tary had been asked to grant an order for the exhuma- tion of the body of the second wife of George Cuapman, the woman who died at the Momument public house, Uoion-street, Southwark, on February 13, last year. This worn an. there can be no doubt whatever, was the daughter of the fate Thomas Parsonage Taylor, of Hill Top Farm, Preston Brook, near Warrinetos, and a near relative of Mr Joseph Taylor, formerly of the Norton Arms Hotel, Warringtoe. The Taylor family Is wiry highly respected in the neigh- bourheod of Preston Brook, the farm mentioned now being worked by a son, Mr H P Taylor. His sistor also resictes on the farm, end the family have resided in or ebent Preston Brook for nearly twenty years. Bessie Taylor who married the man Chapman, for some years prior to her death, had not heel seen much in the dis- trict. She took a position of barmaid and was stationed for some time at York. Where she first met Ctapns in is not known, hut she lived with him at the M uunaent public breve, Southwork, the house he occupied before going to the Crown. The Taylor family spriligs from Lymrn, and it is stated that oe her deathbed the deceased woman ex- preesed to her mother a wish to be taken to the place of hot nativity for burial. for wish•was complied with. She died on February 13, 1901, sad was interred in the graveyard of Lymm Church, the body being taken direct frnm L)ndon by rail. At one tune the family were very well known in 14mm, the late Mr Tailor for some years taking part ms a member of the old Lreial Boare, now supplanted by the Urban Council. in the eevernment of the township. As two decades have almost elapsed since the Taylor family left Lymm, they ate. however, only remembered by the older generation. The grave occupied by the daughter, and now by ' both her parents also, is situated on the right-hand side cf the footpath immediately after entering tho gate. Oa 'ha plain upright stone appea.s the follow' ig, inscrip- tion i—" Thomas Parsonage Taylor, died June 11, 1902, nee 167 years ; also Betsy, his wife, died August 22, 1902, agrq3 73 years ; also their dtugh•,er, Wasie Char- m ii, vrtio died February 13, 1901, aged 36 years " Ii viii be seen, therefore, that tho last two rell'a have been sad ones tor the family. Mr Tayter, senior, was in the early part of the present year run over by a trip and suataineil a fractured leg, from which he never recovered, whilst his wife only surviv Id him afw weeks, the shock of his death probably proving too much for her.

A Constable's Plucky Action._

At G 45 on Thuisday morning. Police Constable Whittaker was on duty in Winwick-road when he noticed a black cab attached to a butcher's handry coming at a wild gallop alon4 the road, near Tanner's-lane. The constable succeeded in getting bold of the bit at the end of the rein lie was dragged across the road, but managed to bring the horse to a standstill. The vehicle, which was in charge of a boy named Stephen Broughton, aged 15. belormed to Mr Mynekvme, butcher, Market- place. When passing over Proghall bridge the horse was startled by a passing engine, and bolted, the boy hating no control whatever over the animal.

An alarming explosion occurred on Wednesday night at the powder mills between Hounslow and Felthaca, where some green power in the process of mixing blew uo and destroyed several sheds. Three distinct explo- sions were heard at intervals of a few seconds, and windows were shaken violently for ra'les round. A watchman was slightly burnt.

div.head: EVENING WORK AT VICTORIA ROAD.
div.p: EVENING WORK AT VICTORIA ROAD.

His Majesty's Inspector submitted the f -flowing report which was considered satisfactory : "The second year's work is producing better results and tne praaptct is much more hopeful It is unfortunate that the number of pupil teachersis so limited ascot toljustify an increase in the teaching staff. The work is very severe. A letter was read from Mr Moulton rrquesting the appoint- ment of an additional teacher for trie Victoria-road boys evening school. Mrs Killcross also desired an additional teacher for the girl.' evening school.—lt was recom- mended that the matter be left in the hands of the Chairman and the Clerk.—Recommended that the Clerk obtain copies of the scale of salaries of assistant teachers adopted by other School Boards. Mr Handly proposed that the minutes be adopted. Mr Norman seconded.
Mr Imison ast3cd if the Board cool; not have the re- sult cf the sub-committee appointed to inquire, accord- ing to the minutes. into the advisability ot the proposed new teachers for Victoria-road ?

' The Chairman replied that if L 136 Board wished it the report could be given. ! Mr Handley said that he and Mr Pritchard attended the school to see really what was the condition of things. They found in the boys school about one hundred in attendance. A fair number of them were grown up men. Some were learning their letters, others the first rules of arithmetic, all of which required individual at- tention. Mr Parr bed a large number in another room who needed his constant attendance. In another room were about forty youths from 14 to 18 years of age,who took the whole cf Mr Brown's attention. In another room Mr Byrne W 49 engaged with persons of a higher grade. They thus came to the conclusion that another teacher wasreally required so that Mr Moulton could assist as it was required and have a general oversight. They recom- mended that Mr Connell and Miss Perkins be appointed as junior assistant teachers. Mr Pritchard seconded and the motion was approved. This was all the buainess of general interest.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Urged by pressure I can no longer withstand, I have reluctantly consented to allow my name to be put forward for your representation. Raving taken a prominent part in tte agitation for the purification of the Cornell. in th effort to lift muni- cipal duties out of the rut of party—in my opinion, the curse of municipal life—it Is unnecessary that I should say I am not in any sense the nominee of either of the two political parties. I sub nit, in short, that it is the duty of the wise citizen to select a man because he is competent, fearless, and honest, and not because he is blue, green or red. Nor do I covet or seek election. I shall not personally canvass a single burgess, nor risk for a single v^te. but if you approve my platform, and think I can serve you. I will undertake, if you will vote for sue and I should be returned, to do whatever an honest but busy man may be expected to do with a single eye to your best Interests and your faithful service. On the other hand. I must add that should I find at any time I cannot give full attention to the duties of the position. I will at once resign it. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient Servant, JAMES DODDS. Bewsey-road, Warrington, 23rd October, 1902.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. 1902, TO THE ELECTORS OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, At the request of a large and influential body of rate- payers, k have again decided to contest the Latchford Ward at the forthcoming Municipal Election. I alll a large ratepayer and employer of labour in the Ward, and pay Trades Union rates of wages,and I should strongly support the giving of Corporation contracts to firms acknowledging this principle in the payment of their warkpeople. Many burgesses, of all shades of opinion and thought, have requested me to come forward. I am also the adopted candidate of the Conservative Association. On the question of Municipal Trading by Aldermen and Councillors with the Corporation I hold very strong opinions, which I have frequently expressed. I am vigorously opposed to these immoral transactions, and if returned shall do ever thing in my power with a view to putting an end to th ""s scandalous state of things, The rates, through he extravagance of the Town Council, have become al most unbearable. It will be my aim to keep the expend tture within bounds, in order that a reduction in the ra tea might be brought about as speedily as possible, since heavy rates mean high rental I will notlupport any compromise between the two political parties. It Is often remarked that Couneillors forget their promises directly the election is over, and It has been stated that I shall do the same if elected. My persistent action, however, during the past two years, ought to be a guarantee as to my future conduct. If returned as your representative I am confident that I shall be able, with the twomised support of many large and influential ratepayers in the town, to carry out the reforms which the Ratepayers have hitherto so hopelessly longed for. Trusting to receive the honour of your votes on atur- day, November let, I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient servant, JOHT: PEMBRRION. Stockton Heath, October 23rd, 1902.

To THE ELECTORS OF FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES Agl) GEFTLEMEN, Having received a most gratifying invitation from Residents in Fairfield Ward, t. quite irrespective of Party," to become a Candidate at the forthcoming Muni- cipal Election. I have decided to accede to their request, and as an INDEPENDENT CANDIDATE now ask you toisuprort me by your vote on November Ist. I am not Ike Nominee of eith-r Political Club, believ- ing as I do that Politics should have no part in Municipal affairs. I have NO AXE TD GRIND and NO PARTY to please. My sole wish would be to please the Electors by doing my duty without fear or favour, and advancing the Interests of the Ward to the utmost of my ability. lam strongly averse to any member of the Council trading with the Corporation either through Limited Companies or otherwise. If elected I shall advocate the Extension of Tramways In the Ward. I am well know tto most of you, having lived in the town all my life, and for the greater part of it in Fairfield Ward. and am therefore thoroughly conversant with its requirements. I make no promises to " Catch Votes" beyond this. viz.. that if you honour me with your confidence I will do my utmost for the Ward in particular, and the town in general. Trusting I shall have your support on November let, I am, yours respectfully, JAMES G. CRAIK. Green Bank, Manchester Road, 23rd October, 1902.

Although I am the representative of the Conservative Association, it shall be my duty to further the wishes of the burgesses of the ward and town, irrespective of any party or Association. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant. JOHN HOSHRTS. October 24th, 19'2.

MUNICIPAL ,GLECTIONS, 1902. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE LATCHFORD WARD. _— LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been requested to stand as a Candidate for your Ward, I beg to appeal to you for your support in return- ing me to serve your interests in the Town Council. I have been a resident in the Latchford Ward for the last sixteen years, and have always publicly taken an Interest in matters affecting the advancement of the Town. If elected, my aim will be to exercise due care in Finance, while maintaining efficiency, and to serve your interests with probity and zeal. Politically It is well known that I am a Conservative, but in this contest I am an Independent Candidate and confidently venture to appeal to all ratepayers for their support and votes. I am ladies and gentlemen, Yours obediently, W. B. ROBERTS. Wllderspool, Oct. 15. 19.2. MUNICIPAL GLECTIONS, 1902. TO THE BURGESSES OF wIET LATCHF ORD TIA ARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.— We venture to appeal to you for your support and vote for Mr. W. B. ROBERTS, of Wilderspool, on Saturday, November Ist. Mr. ROBERTS comes before you as an INDEPEN- DENT CANDIDATE. Though well-known as a Con- servative, so general is the view that he will prove an excellent and useful member of the Town Council, as well as being best qualified and most able to look after the particular interests of this ward, he is receiving the combined support of Liberals and Conservatives. We therefore beg of you to do all you can in MT. Roberts' interest, and above all by making a point of voting early for him on November Ist. We are, ladies and gentlemen. Yours faithfully, GEO. Having been requested by a large number of rate- payers to become a Candidate for the representation of your Ward in the Town Council, I have consented to I place my services at your disposal. Having resided in the Ward for a great number of years, I am intimately acquainted with all your requirements. I shall endeavour to secure cheaper gas, better sanitary arrange- ments, and a continuance of the better paving and light- ing of all the streets and back-pasages in the Ward, so as to improve it from a health and sanitary point of iiew. Living amongst you as 1 do, if you do me the honour to elect me, I shall at all times be ready to per- sonally investigate any subject which you wish to bring to my notice, and do my utmost to promote the best Interests of the burgesses. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours faithfully. JOHN BROPHY. 125, Dallam-lane, Warrington. MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. 1902.—T0 THE ELECTORS OF THE WHI'TECROCS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.— My term of office as the representative of this Ward having expired, I again offer m self as a Candidate at the forthcoming Election. For several years past, through your votes, I have had the honour to represent you. I have endeayoared to dia. charge my duties to the best of my ability with a:sincere desire to promote Tour Welfare and that of the town generally. My interest in all that concerns the working men was I think, shown quite recently when, confronted by some opposition,l proposed in the Town Council and succeeded in obtaining,the recognition of a principle hitherto disre- garded which will be an important factor in the future settlement of all disputes between the Corporation aud their Employees. With reference to finance and the town's expenditure am on the aloe of economy, a strict opponent of waste and extravagance, and in favour of wise and judicious expenditure leading to Municipal progress and efficiency. If again returned as your representative it will be my pleasure to do my duty. Yours truly, JAMES EVANS.

TO THE ELECTORS OF ORFORD WARD LADIEs AND GENTLEMEN,— I have yielded to the request of a number of influential ratepayers to become a candidate for the representation Of your Ward in the Town Council. Having resided In the Ward for ,some years, and worked in it for seventeen years I may fairly claim to know It and its needs thcroughly. By the Bill now before Parliament, the T)wn Council Will become the Authority for Primary. Secondary, and Technical Education. As a headmaster for the past 20 years it has been a part of my daily work to be fully acquainted with acts of Parliament relating to Education, Education Codes, Science and Art Directories, and all matters 'pertaining to education. On these matters I may without egotism, claim to be an expert and I feel confident that if elected I shall be able to render effi- cient service to the town in the great changes that are impending in the control and organization of education. I am a strong advocate for the municipality providing means of reasonable recreation for the people in this part of the town by the provision of a branch reading room and the creating of a proper recreation ground pn the waste space between Winwilk-road and Orford-lane. I am, "44(11P5 and Gentlemen. Yours faithtuily. JOHN UPSON.
